"On the balance of probabilities, I am therefore satisfied that Mr Mourant would not have driven had he been suspended and Mrs Mohammadi's death would therefore have been prevented."

'Difficult to comprehend' authorities weren't notified

Mr Whittle said the fact Mourant had been able to "simply declare he had no medical impediment to driving" despite having a vision condition, raised "concerns about the interactions between his medical assessments and the state's licensing authority".

"Mr Mourant was assessed by three doctors, and all three were aware of his grossly constricted visual fields. However, not one of them notified the Registrar of Motor Vehicles pursuant to an apparent obligation under s 148 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1959," Mr Whittle said.

" I do, admittedly, find it difficult to comprehend how the medical professionals dealing with Mr Mourant considered it appropriate to advise him not to drive, that is, they formed a belief that him driving would be risky, but nevertheless determined not to exercise their duty under s 148. "

Tristan Mourant hit a van, killing Sohaila Mohammadi in January 2022. (ABC News)

That section of the act states that a health professional is required to inform the registrar if a person has a "physical or mental illness, disability of deficiency such that, if the person drove a motor vehicle, the person would be likely to endanger the public".

Mourant pleaded guilty to charges of causing death by dangerous driving, and causing serious harm by dangerous driving.

In October 2024, he was jailed for just over seven years, with a non-parole period of six years, eight months and 13 days.

His licence was also disqualified for 20 years.

Not possible to pull woman from van fire

In his findings, Mr Whittle also found that after the crash, Mrs Mohammadi's death could not have been prevented due to the fire which had engulfed the van her husband, Noor Ahmad, was driving.

He said the intensity of the flames "was severe and engulfed the van so quickly that it was not possible to extricate Mrs Mohammadi".

Mr Whittle also found there was nothing Mr Ahmad — who was also injured in the crash — could have done differently, as he had been driving in a "perfectly reasonable and normal manner" at the time.

"I am therefore satisfied that there were no actions that Mr Ahmad could have taken which could or would have prevented Mrs Mohammadi's death," Mr Whittle said.

He also offered his condolences to Mrs Mohammadi's family, noting that the fact her death "occurred at the hands of an individual who selfishly put his own desires above the safety of all others is deplorable".

"That there were missed opportunities to take him off the road is regrettable," Mr Whittle said.

He recommended that medical colleges, including the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Ophthalmologists, issue communication to members and SA Health medical staff that it was "a mandatory obligation" to notify the registrar when a driver poses a risk to other road users, and that future staff are also made aware of the obligation.

He further recommended the Minister for Infrastructure and Transport similarly provide information and guidance to all other health professionals.

World.title: Coalition vows to scrap VNI West transmission project in Victoria
World.content:
The Victorian Coalition has promised to scrap Labor's controversial VNI West transmission project, 100 days out from the state election in November.

The Liberal and National parties previously committed to pausing and reviewing VNI West after strong opposition from farmers in its path.

Nationals deputy leader Emma Kealy said the Coalition's decision to dump the project made it clear where the parties stand.

"As far as the Nationals and Liberals are concerned, VNI West is dead, buried and cremated," she said.

"We've gone back and had a look at all of the data that surrounds VNI West and it's really clear that the project isn't going to ever stack up."

Anger is palpable among farmers in the path of VNI West. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long)

The proposed transmission line connecting Victoria to the New South Wales grid is estimated to cost between $7.6 billion and $11.4 billion.

It is part of Labor's plan to support renewable energy generation and maintain power reliability.

There is strong and widespread opposition in Victoria's west, particularly among farmers whose land is along the planned route.

The Coalition said it would explore alternative options to keep power generation and prices sustainable.

"We're looking at unlocking our gas reserves, we're looking at extending coal to its technical end of life," Ms Kealy said.

"[We will] make sure we're looking at those renewable projects like the solar parks in Melbourne and other metropolitan areas … [to] capture the energy near to where it's going to be consumed."

Emma Kealy says VNI West does not stack up. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

In a statement, Energy and Resources Minister Jaclyn Symes said the Coalition's pledge to scrap the project was irresponsible.

"Jess Wilson's One Nation-Coalition's reckless decision will destroy electricity reliability across Victoria, guaranteeing blackouts and pushing up power bills," she said.

"Only Labor will build the critical renewable energy infrastructure, including VNI West, needed to deliver cheap power and keep the lights on as our aging coal-fired generators retire."

Ms Symes also questioned whether the Coalition would reintroduce fracking.

"There is no restriction on bringing online new gas supply through conventional means in Victoria," Ms Symes said.

" Is Jess Wilson promising to overturn the ban on fracking in Victoria? "

Jaclyn Symes has questioned whether the Coalition will reintroduce fracking. (ABC News)

The Victorian Farmers Federation has welcomed the Coalition's commitment.

"VNI West has long been a failed project that is tearing apart generational farming families and would rip up some of the best farmland in the country," president Ryan Milgate said.

"You cannot put a dollar figure on the loss of irreplaceable, highly productive farming land or the damage caused when you carve a massive transmission project through established farming operations."

Ryan Milgate has welcomed the Coalition's promise to scrap VNI West. (ABC News: Sean Warren)

While farmers are cheering the Coalition's move, renewable energy and environment groups have slammed it.

Clean Energy Council chief executive Jackie Trad said VNI West was critical to energy security and the replacement of aging coal.

"Cancelling VNI West does not make that closure [of Yallourn] go away. It just decreases the amount of electricity Victorians have access to, inevitably pushing up prices and electricity bills," she said.

"The Coalition says gas will fill the gap, but Victorians deserve to know where that gas is actually going to come from."

Transmission tower and lines on farmland. (Supplied: VicGrid)

Environment Victoria's climate campaign manager Joy Toose said the Coalition's plan would expose Victorians to higher power prices and less reliable electricity.

"Renewables and the transmission that carries them are the only thing actually bringing bills down," she said.

"Cancelling that to burn more gas is a plan for higher bills and blackouts, dressed up as the opposite."

The Coalition has also committed to reviewing and potentially scrapping the Western Renewables Link project, which is further along in the planning process than VNI West.

World.title: Search for missing hiker to enter second week as ADF called in
World.content:
Almost 100 members of the Australian Defence Force (ADF) are helping to search for a bushwalker who has been missing for a week in a national park south-west of Sydney.

The multi-agency search effort for Lily Hooper, 18, started in Nattai National Park on August 12.

Lilly Hooper, 18, has been missing for a week after failing to return from a hike in Nattai National Park. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Reservists from 5th Brigade stationed at Holsworthy Barracks in Sydney joined the effort today.

Army survival instructor Gordon Dedman said many soldiers from the base would be familiar with the difficult terrain.

"You've got personnel, depending on what units are used, familiar with that area south of Holsworthy," he said.

"It's very steep ravines, thick bush, and it can get really cold in winter.

"Even just basic soldiers will have the ability to know that terrain, going through on foot and doing extensive line searches."

Search reaches seven days

Police discovered Ms Hooper's car at the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail on the evening she went missing, but have found no trace of her in the area since.

Mr Dedman said the ready availability of water in the national park worked in the experienced bushwalker's favour.

"It's still early days," he said.

"There is water in the creeks there.

"First-aid issues and clothing are the two big things, because with the proper clothing you can even hug against a tree [to stay warm]."

Survival expert Gordan Dedman said the survival training given to the ADF would help teams navigate the terrain today. (Supplied.)

Police estimate approximately 200 people from the State Emergency Service, Fire and Rescue NSW, VRA Rescue are part of the search effort.

Police have deployed resources including trail bikes, horses, dogs and helicopters.

VRA Rescue NSW Deputy Commissioner Alix Thom said eight volunteers had been sent to camp in the area.

The Nattai National park has dense bushland, deep ravines and high cliffs. (ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale)

"They have a lot of navigation skills, rugged terrain experience, and they're very skilled individuals that we've deployed to that area to assist," she said.

"No matter what the weather is, they won't come back in for the night. They stay out there."

The search continues.

World.title: Patterson's lawyers describe jury hotel arrangement as 'catastrophic'
World.content:
Lawyers for triple murderer Erin Patterson say "catastrophic" jury arrangements during the closing stages of her trial contributed to an unsafe verdict.

Patterson, who served her relatives a beef Wellington laced with death cap mushrooms in 2023, was found guilty of three counts of murder and attempted murder at a trial in Morwell last year.

The 51-year-old, who has always maintained her innocence, filed a conviction appeal made up of seven grounds.

Patterson was today beamed into courtroom one of the Supreme Court in Melbourne via a large screen from the Dame Phyllis Frost women's prison.

Wearing a royal blue jumper, she watched proceedings on a laptop and sat forward listening attentively to the legal arguments.

Don Patterson (left), Heather Wilkinson (centre) and Gail Patterson (right) all died after consuming a beef Wellington meal laced with death cap mushrooms. (ABC News)

In court, Ian Wilkinson, the sole survivor of the fatal lunch, was in the front row of the public gallery and supported by family.

Patterson's estranged husband Simon was not present.

Patterson's barrister Richard Edney described a scenario where jurors deciding the case were sequestered in the same hotel as the case's lead police officer and staff from the Office of Public Prosecutions.

This went against the notion that justice needed to be done, as well as being seen to be done in "perhaps one of the most high-profile criminal trials this state has ever had", Mr Edney said.

"We would describe the sequestration that occurred during it as catastrophic," he said.

However, under questioning from Court of Appeal judges Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd, Mr Edney conceded there was no evidence police or prosecutors directly communicated with jurors, who were being supervised by court staff.

Listen to The Case of podcast | Mushroom Lunch Mushroom Lunch continues to follow all proceedings related to Erin Patterson's triple murder conviction in July 2025.

Mr Edney said communication could have been "non-verbal" and that jurors may have seen the homicide detective, Stephen Eppingstall, through the motel windows.

There was no CCTV obtained from the motel. The court's "jury keepers" and prosecutors also denied anything improper occurred.

The accommodation issue occurred at the time when there was a shortage of hotel rooms in Traralgon, the town next to Morwell, where the trial was being held.

Appeal could take months

The jury eventually found Patterson guilty of murdering in-laws Don and Gail Patterson, along with Gail's sister Heather, and attempting to murder Ian Wilkinson.

Patterson pleaded her innocence and said she did not know mushrooms in the beef Wellington were poisonous.

The appeal is set down for two days.

Erin Patterson listened to proceedings from Dame Phyllis Frost women's prison and appeared in court via video link. (Supplied: Anita Lester)

Prosecutors will get the opportunity to respond to the defence appeal grounds and mount their own appeal against Patterson's jail sentence.

The killer's life sentence included the possibility of parole after 33 years — something the prosecution wants removed.

It could take weeks or months for the judges to rule on the appeals.

Defence accuses prosecution of 'cherry picking'

Patterson's barristers Mr Edney and Veronika Drago today accused the trial prosecutors of conducting an "unfair" cross-examination of the Leongatha mother.

Patterson spent days in the witness box being questioned by then-prosecutor Nanette Rogers SC, at times resulting in tense exchanges between the pair.

"There's a real risk of there being improper inferences left in the minds of the jury," Mr Edney said.

Nanette Rogers SC was the crown prosecutor during Patterson's murder trial in 2025. (AAP: James Ross)

Mr Edney also accused Dr Rogers of "cherry picking" evidence from witnesses when she made her final address to the jury.

He conceded that the same complaint was made by the lead defence barrister at the time, Colin Mandy SC, who chose not to apply for a mistrial.

Judge rulings 'compelled' Patterson to give evidence, court hears

Ms Drago said mobile phone tower evidence from the prosecution, which suggested Patterson may have visited nearby areas where death cap mushrooms were sighted, turned "nothing into something".

She also complained that because of rulings made by the trial judge Patterson was "compelled" to step into the witness box and testify about photos of mushrooms she had taken years before the fatal lunch.

"It compromised her right to silence," Ms Drago said.

Ms Drago stopped short of saying the ruling forced Patterson into the witness box altogether, though.

The appeal continues.

World.title: Why Seoul has called for peace talks to formally end the Korean War
World.content:
South Korea's leader wants to sit down with North Korea and make peace.

North and South Korea are technically still at war as the agreement made to stop fighting on the Korean Peninsula in 1953 was an armistice, not a peace treaty.

Now South Korea has once again called for talks to formally end the Korean War.

So how significant is Seoul's offer and what could it mean for peace on the Korean Peninsula?

North and South Korea are technically still at war. (AFP: Roger-Viollet)

A wide breach to cross

Attempts have been made from both sides to formally end the war over the years, with sticking points including the US military presence in the South and more recently North Korea's nuclear program.

Since taking office last year, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's administration has taken a more conciliatory approach than his hawkish predecessor impeached president Yoon Suk Yeol.

Yoon was sentenced to life in prison earlier this year on charges of rebellion over his attempt to put the country under military rule.

Jay Song, an honorary associate professor from Australian National University, said the centre-left Lee government had a pro-engagement peace policy and had not given up on unification "one day".

"Ending the war first, peace building next and finally if conditions are met, try one Korea," she said.

On the other side of the demilitarised zone, North Korea has abandoned its official aim of unification in recent years, with leader Kim Jong Un declaring South Korea as the North's "most hostile state".

In 2024, the authoritarian dictatorship said it would permanently block its border with South Korea and boost its front-line defence posture to cope with "confrontational hysteria" by South Korean and US forces.

"The important thing here is that the nature of the inter-Korean relations remains hostile so that Pyongyang can continue to develop its nuclear weapons and missiles," Dr Song said.

North Korea expert Leonid Petrov said nuclear weapons were a non-negotiable for the North as they served as a guarantee of regime survival.

"Any contact, exchange, or cooperation with South Korea poses serious security risks to the North Korean political system because such engagement undermines its legitimacy and its myths of superiority," said Dr Petrov, who teaches Korean studies at the Australian National University.

Korean Liberation Day is celebrated in both the North and the South. (Reuters: Lee Jin-man)

How significant was the speech?

Mr Lee extended the most recent olive branch during a speech on Saturday to mark Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule.

Liberation Day is celebrated by both North and South Korea, though with diverging narratives.

"Let us put down our intentions to threaten each other and begin discussions to end the long-running war as the directly involved parties," Mr Lee said.

"Through this, it may also be possible to discuss effective measures to halt the advancement of North Korea's nuclear capabilities."

Dr Song said without a formal peace treaty war could resume at any time.

Ministers tread carefully as Trump scales back drills Australia and Japan's defence ministers discuss the rapidly expanding defence ties between the two countries.

"In fact, there have been many clashes and skirmishes at the land and maritime borders," she said.

"People living on the Korean Peninsula have internalised this unstable conflict situation for more than 70 years.

"Mistrust, surveillance and violence have been normalised.

"In this context, President Lee's call for ending the war and establishing a peace regime is significant."

Alexander Hynd, a lecturer at the University of Melbourne's Asia Institute, said some people saw the peace treaty talks as "unfinished business".

"For others, this is low-hanging fruit that can be helpful in kickstarting more meaningful inter-Korean talks and future cooperation," he said.

"North Korea has so far largely ignored South Korean President Lee's attempts to improve relations since he was elected last June," he added.

'We can achieve peace'

For some members of Australia's Korean diaspora, Mr Lee's calls for peace talks has been decades in the making.

Sun Jung from Werribee in Melbourne said she was "delighted" when she heard.

"This approach has been lacking for so many years," Ms Jung told the ABC.

" I really believe that through dialogue and communication, we can achieve peace. "

Sun Jung was "delighted" when she heard about Lee Jae Myung's speech. (ABC News: Angelica Silva)

Ms Jung said her family carried the war inside them. Her father was around 15 years old when it began — his brothers and his parents were affected too.

"They all went through the war. They suffered," she said.

"They've seen it all, from poverty to ashes from all the burning.

"People there have suffered enough."

But while Ms Jung welcomed the prospect of peace talks, she said a treaty was only the first step.

"To me, peace is not just about the absence of war or a formal paper that needs to be signed," she said.

"It is about respecting human life and every individual's right to live."

Ms Jung, who became a citizen in 2005, has lived in Australia longer than she has in South Korea.

While she said that she did not follow Korean current events "all the time", moments like Mr Lee's comments pulled her back in.

"In my blood and in my heart is Korea," she said.

"So, I like to know what's happening there, and I want to contribute in any way."

North Korea has "permanently" shut its border with South Korea. (AP: Lee Jin-man)

A bid to restart diplomacy

Jenny Town, senior fellow and director of 38 North at the Stimson Center, told the ABC's The World South Korea had long been trying to figure out how to restart diplomacy with North Korea.

The North's decision to label South Korea a permanent hostile state meant the political infrastructure that had allowed negotiations had been severed.

"They keep trying to find ways to rebuild this relationship, knowing that they need to lower tensions … they don't want this constant pressure and tension," she said.

"With the Liberation Day speech, I think this was their way of saying that they don't have to be in a permanently hostile arrangement with each other."

Nonetheless, Dr Town said there still was not a consensus in South Korea on formally ending the war because it had become so tied to the relationship with the US.

"If you see the war as a function of maintaining the alliance, then the status quo is preferable over severing the alliance as a whole," she said.

"But technically the alliance is not contingent on the war continuing. It is a separate agreement … and should be dealt with separately than the actual formal ending of the war itself."

Donald Trump says he and Kim Jong Un understand each other. (AP: Susan Walsh)

Could peace talks actually go ahead?

North Korea has yet to officially respond to Mr Lee's outreach.

Complicating matters, North Korea has in recent times formed increasingly close ties with Russia while the United States under President Donald Trump has been sowing doubt about his commitment to supporting South Korea.

Dr Petrov said Mr Lee's proposal was "falling on deaf ears" because Mr Kim had a better deal with Russia.

"These days, Moscow is offering cash, energy, and advanced military technology — effectively making international sanctions irrelevant — in exchange for North Korean troops and conventional weapons to be used against Ukraine," he said.

US allies question Washington's reliability President Donald Trump's late call to "substantially reduce" military exercises with South Korea has prompted speculation he is courting a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

On Sunday, Mr Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back planned joint military exercises with South Korea, saying it declined to help denuclearise Iran and citing his good relationship with Mr Kim.

The US on Tuesday local time confirmed the exercises would conclude on August 21, a week earlier than scheduled.

Dr Hynd said he did not view Mr Lee's offer as likely to lead to a major breakthrough in inter-Korean relations.

"If anything, it is more about steadying the ship and locking in the status quo, at a time when President Lee's major challenge is how to deal with President Trump's unpredictability and general ambivalence towards the US-South Korea alliance."

Dr Song said peace was not easy to achieve on the Korean Peninsula.

"It's not just the two Koreas' problem but intertwined with great powers around them: the US, China, Russia and Japan," she said.

"It appears the only party that desperately wants peace is South Korea at the moment.

"The others all want a flashpoint in that region to grow their own power and influence."

Additional reporting by Girish Sawlani

World.title: UK's new PM messaged with person claiming to be Trump's chief of staff
World.content:
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has confirmed he exchanged messages with someone pretending to be US President Donald Trump's chief of staff.

Speaking to reporters during a visit to central England on Tuesday, Mr Burnham said he was not embarrassed by the incident, which was raised with the White House.

Here's what to know.

What happened?

Politico first reported on Monday that Mr Burnham engaged with "a few messages" sent by someone impersonating White House chief of staff Susie Wiles via an unspecified communication channel.

Mr Burnham said he became suspicious of the contact and reported the incident.

The British embassy in Washington then raised the matter with the White House, according to two sources cited by Politico.

The White House did not immediately respond to an ABC request for comment.

Andy Burnham with West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker during his visit to Wolverhampton Bus Station on Tuesday. (Reuters: Hannah McKay/Pool)

What was said in the messages?

We don't have the details.

The messages have not been released to the public, and Downing Street has declined to say when the exchange occurred or how many messages were sent.

But Mr Burnham has said nothing sensitive had been discussed during the "minimal exchange".

"Nothing of consequence, and actually, quickly I realised that this needed to be reported, and I did so," he said during a visit to the central English city of Wolverhampton.

Have there been security incidents like this before?

Yes.

Federal authorities began investigating a similar effort to impersonate Ms Wiles in 2025, according to reports published in May of that year.

The FBI probe came after an unknown individual who posed as Ms Wiles contacted prominent Republicans and business executives.

Susie Wiles told associates last year that her phone had been hacked. (Reuters: Daniel Heuer)

Ms Wiles told associates her personal phone had been hacked and the information on her contact list exposed.

Several people who received messages from the person claiming to be Ms Wiles reportedly became suspicious when the impersonator attempted to move the conversations to Telegram.

Mr Burnham is not the first British leader to fall victim to a hoax call, either.

Boris Johnson gaffe Britain's Foreign Secretary Boris Johnson talks international relations and rude poetry with a hoax caller.

Boris Johnson talked about sanctions against Russia during a hoax call that lasted 18 minutes while he was foreign secretary in 2018.

And former prime minister David Cameron fell victim to hoaxes in 2024 and 2015.

In the more recent incident, he spoke with someone impersonating former Ukrainian president Petro Poroshenko via a call and text messages.

While he was prime minister in 2015, Downing Street connected him with a caller pretending to be the head of the UK Government Communications Headquarters.

How has Burnham responded?

Asked on Tuesday, local time, whether he was embarrassed at being taken in, Mr Burnham said: "No, I'm not."

"I handled it in the right way. All politicians are receiving these pressures and these challenges, but I did everything right," he said.

He added that the "correct action" was taken in both the UK and US.

How can you spot a scam caller?

While this hoax call may have been tailored to Mr Burnham, scammers can target anyone.

Here are some quick warning signs that a caller may be a scammer, according to Scamwatch:

They ask for personal or financial information: payment, or for you to move money between accounts your password, PIN, one-time code, or some other security information credit card or banking details to process a refund or other "overpayment"

They want you to install software or access a secure account on your mobile phone or computer

They threaten you with immediate arrest, deportation, or blackmail

They suggest you or your accounts have been hacked or involved in fraud

They tell you about a way to make quick, easy money with little risk or effort.

ABC/AFP

World.title: South Australian couple missing in Tasmania
World.content:
Tasmania Police has deployed search and rescue teams in the state's north-west after an elderly couple visiting from South Australia was reported missing.

Clementina, 81, and her 79-year-old partner Peter were last seen at 2:30pm yesterday in Milabena, 44 kilometres west of Burnie, in Tasmania's north.

The couple was visiting family in Tasmania and had embarked on an afternoon of sightseeing, with their destination unknown.

Peter, pictured in an image released by police. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

Police believe they may be with their vehicle, a silver Honda CR-V with South Australian registration S744ACB.

Police believe the pair may have intended to travel to the Penguin, Gawler and Gunns Plains area.

The couple was first reported missing last night after they did not return home as planned and their family were unable to get in contact with them.

The silver 2008 Honda CRV driven by the South Australian couple in Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmania Police)

Unfavourable weather marring search

Clementina is described as about 149 centimetres tall, of solid build and was last seen wearing a green sherpa-lined hoodie, blue or black pants and black lace-up shoes.

Peter is described as of solid build, with grey hair, glasses, no facial hair and about 170 cm tall.

He was wearing a navy blue hoodie, navy blue track pants and New Balance sneakers when last seen by family members.

The police helicopter has been requested to aid the search, but unfavourable weather conditions in the area have prevented it from assisting so far.

Anyone with information or who may have seen the couple or their silver car is being urged to contact Tasmania Police on 131 444.

World.title: Indigenous academic abused by members of pro-Palestinian movement
World.content:
Prominent academic and advocate for Indigenous Australians Marcia Langton says she has been subjected to abuse and labelled a "zio" by members of the pro-Palestinian movement.

Dr Langton appeared before the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Wednesday to discuss the role of education in tackling all forms of racism and hate, including antisemitism.

She said she had been subjected to racism and abuse because of her support for Jewish Australians.

"I've been labelled a zio by the pro-Palestine movement in Melbourne. I've had people pull out of panels that I was listed to speak at … my car's windows were smashed," she said.

"Labelling me as a zio … I'm therefore made voiceless in the debate.

"Because as much as I might be horrified and oppose what's happening in Gaza … the foul treatment of Jewish Australians cannot be justified by saying that Israel is doing this in Gaza."

Childcare fostering social cohesion

The commission also heard from a Jewish Australian woman working to foster social cohesion in her childcare centre, which has about 70 per cent non-Jewish families on its books.

Known as AEA, the woman said the centre introduces children to Jewish culture by creating sensory experiences influenced by tradition.

She said the aim of this was to celebrate difference, while also highlighting the values and experiences children of different cultures share with their friends.

"There is no intention for a non-Jewish child to adopt that practice … but what it is is connecting on those shared values," she said.

For example, AEA said each Friday children participate in challah baking, with the loaves of bread taken home to be shared with family.

"This is a very distinct tradition … but the values underneath that is something we all share. That idea of sharing food with family," she said.

AEA said work was underway to develop a pilot program based on the centre's model.

World.title: Army joins search for missing Sydney bushwalker, 18
World.content:
The army has joined the search for missing Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper, a week after she failed to return from a trip to the Nattai National Park in the NSW Southern Highlands.

Close to 100 Australian Defence Force members joined the search on Wednesday, combining with other emergency services who have been looking for the 18-year-old since she went missing a week ago. Drones and helicopters have also been scouring the national park from the sky.

Lily Hooper, 18, is missing after going hiking in the Nattai National Park. NSW Police

Hooper was last seen leaving her home in Oakdale in Sydney’s south-west at 8am on Wednesday last week to go on a hike through the national park. Throughout the day, she remained in contact with her family, but they raised the alarm when she had not returned by 10pm.

Police found her Hyundai parked at the bottom of the challenging Bonnum Pic trail that night.

World.title: ‘I wish I got injured instead of him’: Brotherly love ahead of Trbojevic comeback
World.content:
Jake Trbojevic has paid tribute to brother Tom as he embarks on another comeback, saying most players in his position would have written off the year. Tom Trbojevic is a huge addition to a Manly side that remains a mathematical possibility of squeaking into the finals if they beat Newcastle at McDonald Jones Stadium on Saturday. The Sea Eagles haven’t won a game since their captain suffered his latest hamstring injury, in round 20. However, the fullback will be a welcome addition to a side that has lost halfback Joey Walsh to a fractured jaw. Another Trbojevic, youngest sibling Ben, also returns from injury. “I’ll be honest, it is tough, it’s really tough,” Jake Trbojevic said about playing without Tom.



“I’ve got a lot of respect for Tom, obviously being my brother and all that, but the way he goes about things – he is a true professional. “Everyone says that about people, but he genuinely is. Sometimes I wish it was me who got injured instead of him, because he puts in 10 times more work than anyone else to get his body right, and he’s just been very unlucky. Tom Trbojevic, Jake Trbojevic and Ben Trbojevic Getty Images “It’s very hard to see, particularly being his older brother. Not only that, selfishly I want him out on the field because he makes us better, you know? So, it is tough, but I’m happy for him that he’s very resilient and keeps working hard. These things don’t hold him back. “A lesser man would probably say, ‘You know what, I’ll just sit the year out and come back next year,’ but he’s fighting. He wants to be out there, he wants to lead this club, and that’s great.”



If Tom Trbojevic’s return is successful he could put himself into contention for Australia selection for the end-of-year World Cup. Much will depend on how he and Manly perform in coming weeks, although it’s unlikely the club will feature in the post-season. “There’s always a chance,” Jake Trbojevic said. “Tom wants to play for Manly, it doesn’t matter what’s on the line, he wants to be out there. He’s the captain of this club for a reason, and we love having him out there. The Northern Beaches loves having him out there. We’re better for it. Tom Trbojevic. Getty “So, it doesn’t matter what’s on the line—whether it’s finals or no finals—we want him out there, he wants to be out there, and he works extremely hard, so he deserves to be out there. We’re going to go out there, put in a great performance, and he’s going to lead us well. Hopefully, we can keep improving and turn this around.” Manly winger Jason Saab said Tom Trbojevic’s return would give the team a confidence boost.



“He’s a world-class player,” Saab said. “He’s had a tough run with injuries this year, but whenever he’s been fit and played the full game, he’s always had an impact. “We’re a better team when the Trbojevics are playing.” ‘Proud day for NRL’: Storm valued at $150m after sale goes through Adrian Proszenko



The Melbourne Storm has been valued at more than $150 million after the world’s second-biggest investment firm bought a majority share of the club. After an exhaustive process to find the right partner, the Storm has completed a landmark transaction with EQT, a Swedish firm with more than $333 billion in assets under management. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images The sale puts the Storm alongside Collingwood and the Brisbane Broncos as one of Australia’s top sporting franchises, just after the NRL brokered a $5.3 billion broadcast deal. Storm chair Matt Tripp – who remains a co-owner alongside Bart Campbell, Gerry Ryan, Tom Carroll and Brett Ralph – said the deal will elevate one of Australia’s top-performing sports clubs even higher.



“I’m really proud that a firm like EQT, who are a serious blue-chip investment company, has chosen us as the team in Australia that they want to invest in,” Tripp said. “That’s a credit to our people and the work that’s gone on over the last 27 years and the 13 years I’ve been involved as a club. “I’ve watched people work tirelessly at the Storm. Off the back of that, EQT recognised that and wanted to be part of that. It’s a really proud day for the club and the NRL more broadly. I think the NRL should be happy that a club has attracted the attention of a company like EQT.” The deal, which will result in EQT earning board seats, is subject to Australian Rugby League Commission approval. Tripp will remain chair, while other key positions will remain the same. “Absolutely status quo,” Tripp said. “I’m still the largest shareholder after EQT and I’m as committed as I’ve ever been. It wouldn’t matter if I owned one per cent of 100 per cent, I’m still as passionate and my desire to drive this club doesn’t waiver …



“These guys own the IMG Academy, which will be really beneficial for us. Related Article NRL 2026 Why a top-two finish by the NZ Warriors could cost NRL $3m “It’s one of the biggest academies in the world, they effectively groom and produce through their pathways academy in the US the best of the best in gridiron, basketball, baseball and the like. “In terms of sports science and everything that goes on that is best in class, we feel we can benefit from that and our new partners will assist us. “They are also huge investors in the AI space and data and hopefully some of that can be transformed into improving areas of the club.”



Latrell ‘a chance’ to make long-awaited return Christian Nicolussi Latrell Mitchell could make a long-awaited return for South Sydney this weekend, with coach Wayne Bennett admitting: “He’s a chance. He’ll still have to get through a couple of training sessions, but he’s some chance.” Bennett said last week Mitchell was likely to be held back for the penultimate week of the season – a round-26 clash against the Gold Coast Titans – but welcomed the prospect of having Mitchell back a week earlier, especially if his body could cope with a few opposed sessions. Latrell Mitchell could make his long-awaited return from injury against the Warriors on Saturday. Steven Siewert



Mitchell’s season looked over a few weeks ago, but he again trained away from the group on a soggy Monday morning as he overcomes a nerve issue in his lower back, which is causing problems down his leg and calf. The 29-year-old injured his back in an outstanding individual performance against Newcastle in round nine, then missed a week before aggravating it against the Dolphins during Magic Round. He hasn’t played since. Should Mitchell’s name be included on the team sheet on Tuesday, Bennett hinted he was unlikely to start, and would be eased into the game off the bench. Tallis Duncan has been playing at left centre in Mitchell’s absence, but is even more effective in the back row, which he will do when Mitchell returns. Latrell Mitchell stretches out at a wet Heffron Park on Monday morning. Steven Siewert



South Sydney need to win one of their remaining three games to cement a spot in the finals, and having a player such as Mitchell available would be a huge boost. The Rabbitohs host the high-flying New Zealand Warriors on Saturday at Accor Stadium, the Sydney Olympic Park venue where they have not lost a game this season. “I don’t know how far off he [Mitchell] is – the physios have a better understanding of that – but he was out there today doing strides … he’s a step closer again,” outside back Campbell Graham said on Monday. South Sydney are looking to continue their unbeaten run at Accor Stadium against the Warriors this weekend. Steven Siewert “Whenever he’s ready to go, we’ll more than welcome him back. We need to keep building as a group; we want to be a well-oiled machine by the time he’s back so he can come in and do his thing.



“He’s handled this situation well. And I’ve been there before where there’s no definite light at the end of the tunnel in terms of when you’ll be playing again. It’s a tough spot to be in. “But he’s full of energy, comes in every day smiling, and he’s great to have around the place.” Graham played his “veteran’s card” to join the rehab group on Monday as part of “load management” to avoid any fresh calf injuries. “I was stoked to get through the game last Friday,” he said. “I’m not out of the woods just yet, and I still have to manage my training loads.” No Red V lifeline as Sloan seeks Super League answers



Dan Walsh Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan says he has been “left in the dark” about the future of Castleford coach Ryan Carr, as St George Illawarra rule out extending an NRL lifeline to him and teammates Damien Cook and Mat Feagai if they look to back out of their Super League deals. Sloan conceded after the Dragons’ two-point win over Wests Tigers on Sunday that he has had second thoughts about his move to Castleford given the uncertainty around Carr’s position. Carr was a key reason Sloan signed a two-year deal with the club last month. Carr, who coached Sloan as an assistant and interim head coach at the Dragons, has been absent from Castleford for the past two weeks after the club launched an investigation into the 38-year-old with little detail or public explanation as to why. Castleford head of football Chris Chester has spoken to the Dragons trio and told them they remain in the club’s plans for next season regardless of Carr’s situation.



Loading St George Illawarra have moved on in their roster planning for 2027 and have privately conveyed that they do not have room for Sloan, Cook and Feagai in their salary cap after a significant recruitment and retention spree. “It definitely puts a big dent in things for me, I’ll be honest,” Sloan said. “Carry was a big reason why I signed over there. “Obviously we had a relationship here at the Dragons and I don’t really know the situation with him. We’ve been left in the dark. “I’m really excited to go over there if Carry is there, but I just don’t know if that’s going to be the case there. Hopefully I’ll find out soon what’s going on and they make a decision.



Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan. Getty Images “I have thought about [trying to stay in the NRL], but I also have to keep playing good footy here to finish the season on a high.” Sloan, 24, has been playing with a new lease on life since Dean Young took charge of the Dragons, scoring eight tries in his past eight games. His time under predecessor Shane Flanagan was far less consistent with several demotions to reserve grade, and 18 months ago he was given permission to explore an early exit from the joint-venture. Immortal Andrew Johns has argued Sloan is “too good a player to be leaving the NRL at this age”, but the Indigenous All Stars representative acknowledged his form in previous years hadn’t left him with many options.



Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Twelve months ago, the Knights were heading for the wooden spoon. Holbrook must be coach of the year Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist “I didn’t really have much [many options] in the NRL, and nothing really made sense, you know, to play in another jersey in the NRL,” Sloan said. “But Joey’s always been really good to me since I came into first grade and to be getting a fair rap from someone who has done everything in the game, I hold that in such respect. At the moment, I’ve got the Super League deal and at the end of it, I’ll only be 26. I’ve been in first grade since I was 18 so no matter what happens, I’d say I’ve got a lot of NRL left in me.”

World.title: Erin Patterson appeal LIVE: Mushroom killer seeks to challenge guilty verdict
World.content:
Crown prosecutor Jeremy McWilliams is now responding to Erin Patterson’s second appeal ground.

Specifically, her lawyers argue:

The cell tower evidence and evidence of death cap mushroom sightings in Loch and Outtrim posted to iNaturalist should not have been adduced in the applicant’s trial as the evidence was not (i) relevant or (ii) the probative value of that evidence was outweighed by its unfair prejudice and the admission of that evidence occasioned a substantial miscarriage of justice.

McWilliams has just gone through some of this contested evidence in detail as he argued it was used appropriately in Patterson’s trial.

“No such argument was made in relation to the iNaturalist evidence in the trial,” McWilliams said.

“The response is that this evidence was part of a collection of evidence which, taken together, demonstrated that the applicant had opportunity to deliberately source death cap mushrooms at a time close to the lunch, and on the prosecution case, did so.”

World.title: Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRetail Opinion Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 19, 2026 — 3:50pm

August 19, 2026 — 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Punch-drunk retailers are attempting to lift themselves off the mat as consumers give them a dose of their own financial reality, keeping cash in their pockets. At the halfway mark of this year’s earnings season, the shareholder jury has spoken – the discretionary retail sector is in an unambiguous slump. Investors are just tapping out. The cyclical retail sector will eventually recover, but the trigger isn’t on the near-term horizon. Breville executes a tariff workaround. Meanwhile, consumers face a perfect storm of cost-of-living pressures thanks to interest rate rises, fuel prices, Middle East war-fuelled inflation and stalling real wages growth. Tumbling house prices and a lack of real estate turnover are the rotten cherry on top. To date, just one major listed retailer, Breville, has stopped short of flagging a performance warning – while releasing a result that included strong sales, albeit with earnings that were shy of pitch perfect.



The company’s financial performance had been buffeted by Donald Trump’s moveable feast on tariffs, which had pushed the appliance maker to move its manufacturing base out of China. Despite this disruption, the company posted a 1.7 per cent profit gain, thanks to what it described as the resilient premium consumer. Related Article Opinion

Global economy China’s breakneck plan to safeguard its future But the market is viewing any weakness with suspicion and isn’t taking any prisoners. Breville’s shares were hammered by about 5 per cent on Wednesday. Discretionary retail companies are watching their share prices tumble, as a conga line of chief executives admit that sales momentum has at best stalled, or at worst fallen off a cliff. Over the past five days, the consumer discretionary index has fallen more than 5 per cent compared with the ASX200, which is 1.7 per cent softer.



Sales from some of our most popular and resilient brands, including Peter Alexander, JB Hi-Fi and Temple & Webster, hit a wall either in the final quarter to June or in the six weeks since. And in the department store space, Myer has spoken of cost-of-living pressures driving down consumer sentiment, while David Jones’ move to further extend payment terms to suppliers speaks volumes about how it is travelling. JB Hi-Fi, which has been a consistent strong performer in the sector, flagged July total sales for its Australian stores were 1.8 per cent softer, with comparable sales growth falling 2.9 per cent. That is a significant reversal in growth from where it was a year ago. Myer has spoken of cost-of-living pressures driving down consumer sentiment. iStock Its other brand, The Good Guys, was 12 per cent lower in the early weeks of the new financial year, with comparable sales growth falling the same amount.



Homewares and furniture retailer Temple & Webster revealed a shock 62 per cent plunge in net profit after significant items, lowered its guidance, and warned revenue was down 13 per cent since the start of the 2027 financial year. It was the recent trading slide that spooked investors, who rewarded it with a near-18 per cent one-day share price collapse. It isn’t just that the consumers have all but closed their wallets, but one retailer after the next says that only discounts will entice shoppers to buy. So even if sales have held up, discounting is crunching margins and eating away at the profit line. It is difficult to find any near-term factors that will restore consumer confidence, given the odds are still in favour of another interest rate increase later this year and the turbulence playing out in the Middle East, which will keep a floor under petrol prices. The war will also feed into higher wholesale prices and further supply chain congestion. But how can retailers pass on these costs with higher consumer prices when shoppers refuse to transact unless goods are on sale?



Even those value investors looking for bargains might hold fire until retail stocks get even cheaper. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.
