World.title: Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies Nick McKenzie Updated August 19, 2026 — 3:39pm ,first published 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A senior executive of Australian infrastructure giant BMD has been accused of secretly meeting violent members of a Melbourne bikie gang in a Brisbane sushi restaurant as part of a plot to threaten a CFMEU activist blamed for causing problems on an Albanese government-funded project. The revelations have prompted the Labor-backed CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby to issue a fresh call for government action to combat the “complete failure of the regulatory system”, while calling on companies with alleged links to bikie gangs and the underworld to “clean up” their backyards. BMD manager Robert Pickard has also been accused in a Queensland inquiry of attempting to cover up the incident after the CFMEU crane driver complained that the leader of a three-man Melbourne bikie crew had threatened to burn down his house and murder his family during a subsequent confrontation on the $350 million Centenary Bridge project. Counsel assisting the Queensland Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU, Eddy Gisonda KC, suggested on Wednesday afternoon that the terrifying stand-over incident occurred a short time after Pickard had met the bikie trio at a sushi shop a short stroll from the bridge redevelopment.



Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies But while being questioned by Gisonda, Pickard repeatedly denied allegations that he knew of or witnessed the alleged Comanchero gang standover on June 5, 2024. He also dismissed suggestions he had met the bikies at the sushi shop or coordinated the alleged standover with the owner of BMD’s security subcontractor, Melbourne company Host. Pickard’s denials came after Gisonda presented a detailed circumstantial case to back up his accusation that Pickard and BMD’s human resources chief, Steve Thomas, appeared to have played a key role in the suspected Comanchero standover of CFMEU-affiliated crane driver Cody Raymond, a man blamed for helping the construction union target BMD. Evidence aired by Gisonda before Commissioner Stuart Wood included receipts showing that one of the three bikies had purchased sushi just minutes after Pickard and Thomas had placed orders at the sushi shop. A short time after that, Pickard and Thomas can be seen on CCTV walking towards the Centenary Bridge project as they are trailed by three Comancheros and Melbourne businessman Gary Samuel, the BMD security subcontractor who was hired to counter an aggressive campaign by the CFMEU targeting BMD.



Pickard disagreed with Gisonda’s suggestion that he and Thomas had led the bikies to the work site at a distance to “to make sure the coast was clear” before Raymond was approached and threatened. Phone data presented by Gisonda also revealed repeated contact or attempted contact between Samuel and both Pickard and Thomas around the time Samuel was picking up the three Melbourne bikies from Brisbane airport, as well as just after what the barrister alleged was a secret rendezvous at the sushi outlet. During the hearing, Wood appeared to accept that Samuel had engineered the bikie standover in retaliation for the conduct of the CFMEU. “It makes sense for Mr Samuel to do this,” Wood suggested, referring to the use of the three feared bikie identities.



“It might be quite unlawful ... [but he had been] taking a knife to a gun fight and he wants to improve the tactics” in respect of BMD’s strategy, he said, to resist CFMEU pressure and in light of the indifference of state authorities to union conduct. “I am not saying it excuses him … But it gives a rational explanation for what he did,” Wood said of Samuel. Rob Pickard (right), General Manager, Queensland and Northern Territory, BMD Constructions is seen being questioned by Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC (left) during the Commission of Inquiry. AAPIMAGE During the hearing, Wood also queried why BMD had told police in November 2024 that CCTV of the bikie incident was no longer available, given the company had provided the vision to Wood’s commission earlier this year. Wood also asked Gisonda to make inquiries about whether it was unlawful for a company or person to “deliberately or inadvertently mislead the police”. But Pickard dismissed the claim that he or BMD were party to a bikie threat plot or that Pickard had sought to “deflect” attention away from his own or Samuel’s role in allegedly coordinating the potentially criminal act.



Wednesday’s hearing will ultimately inform Wood as he weighs whether the circumstantial evidence gathered by Gisonda and the Queensland Police investigators assisting his inquiry is strong enough to allow Wood to make an adverse finding about Pickard or BMD’s involvement in the bikie plot. Gisonda opened the hearing on Wednesday by revealing that law enforcement agencies suspected the Comancheros of seeking to build a construction empire via front companies and by infiltrating union ranks. Queensland’s Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU has laid bare the involvement of the Comancheros in the construction industry. Getty Images He claimed police intelligence, including extensive phone data, indicated the Comanchero bikie gang had in early 2024 embarked on a concerted effort to do this in both Victoria and Queensland. According to Gisonda, this effort involved the now former Melbourne-based Comanchero boss Bemir Saracevic. Saracevic is the same bikie figure Gisonda identified as allegedly leading the standover of Raymond.



Gisonda also tabled union-backed enterprise bargaining agreements allegedly secured by Comanchero-linked building firms in Victoria, including an EBA signed off by the CFMEU administration last month and by the Australian Workers’ Union in 2025. A separate investigation by The Age has established that basic due diligence should have revealed to both unions that these firms had business links to the Comancheros: one had previously been refused a licence to operate by Victoria’s Labour Hire Authority, while both had clear links to the wife of Saracevic. Bemir Saracevic. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU In a statement, Crosby told this masthead that the EBA his union had recently granted a firm now alleged to be Comanchero-linked was intended to protect workers. The CFMEU administrator said it was up to government, and not the CFMEU, to prevent underworld infiltration. “The Administrator has called for a Fit and Proper Persons Test to be applied to participants in the construction industry. It’s time the industry was cleaned up. It’s time to stop blaming workers for the complete failure of the regulatory system. It’s not the job of the union to clean up the industry,” he said.



“We’ll clean up our backyard – it’s time for employers to clean up theirs.” Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Idiots in Victoria’ holding back CFMEU: Administrator blasts former union bosses, demands reform The Queensland hearing has also placed immense scrutiny on BMD, which is currently working on Victoria’s Eastern Freeway upgrade and other Big Build projects. In Sydney, it is working on the new international airport in Western Sydney. In July, the Crisafulli government in Queensland announced that BMD had won the contract to undertake early works for the new Brisbane Stadium Olympics venue. Asked by this masthead about the evidence heard at the commission suggesting BMD associated with underworld-linked figures in the alleged Centenary Bridge stand-over incident and whether BMD’s internal investigation into the matter was adequate, the company’s spokesperson said: “BMD has additional representatives to appear over the coming days and it would be premature for us to comment.”



The revelations at the Queensland inquiry give Australians a taste of what is likely to be unveiled at the promised and upcoming Victorian royal commission. Many of the key subjects discussed at this week’s hearings in Brisbane are from Melbourne and are variously entrenched in both Victoria’s underworld and its building sector. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I was a terrible player’: Renshaw bids to end opener roulette a decade after baby-faced debut
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I was a terrible player’: Renshaw bids to end opener roulette a decade after baby-faced debut Daniel Brettig Updated August 19, 2026 — 3:36pm ,first published August 19, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Matt Renshaw was still in something of a daze as he picked up his bags to resume life as a Test cricketer, a decade after being a “little baby” in the national team. Renshaw was at home in Brisbane with his wife Josie and their two young children on Monday night when the call came from selection chair George Bailey, telling him to get ready to join Australia as they try to overturn a surprise defeat by Bangladesh in Darwin. Matt Renshaw looks happy to be recalled to the Australian test team, especially given the match against Bangladesh is in Mackay, where he has made big scores in the past. Getty Images for Cricket Australia “I wasn’t really expecting it, so when the name came up on my phone I was quite surprised,” Renshaw, 30, told this masthead. “I look back at photos of myself 10 years ago and see a little baby playing Test cricket. It was pretty crazy, but hopefully this time getting the opportunity, I’ll be in a lot better mindset and a lot better frame.”



Despite being part of the 19-man training squad in Brisbane for six weeks leading up to the first Test, Renshaw had no inkling he was about to be returned to the top of the order, particularly given that Jake Weatherald had beaten him to a Cricket Australia contract. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection? “It was amazing preparation for me to get better,” he said. “That’s how I tried to use those couple of weeks, try to get better getting to face some of the best bowlers in the world three times a week was pretty cool. That’s all I saw it as, and fortunately I’m here now.” A host of players have been tried at the top of Australia’s batting order over the past decade, but none have been able to match Usman Khawaja, David Warner or more recently Travis Head. Renshaw, with an average of 36 over his first 10 Tests before sporadic appearance since, came closest. Renshaw now expects to open alongside Head, but he returns to the team with a raft of recent experience in other positions, not least in Bangladesh in a white-ball series earlier this year.



“I love opening,” Renshaw said. “I love the satisfaction that it brings when you perform after opening, but I feel like it’s held me in good stead doing it all around the order. “The white-ball stuff’s given me a different mindset and a little bit of freedom to express myself, to be able to bat and learn different things. Time down the middle order for Queensland gave me a bit more confidence as well.” Matt Renshaw with Pete Handscomb after his first Test hundred in January 2017. Getty It was against Bangladesh in 2017 that Renshaw ended his first stint in the Test side. Based on the numbers alone, it was a harsh call at the time, but having grown much as a person and a cricketer since, Renshaw feels well grounded for his chance to become Usman Khawaja’s long-term replacement at the top. “I know if Renshaw is picked that he is in the best space right now to have a crack at Australia again and be ready to score runs,” Khawaja said of Renshaw last summer. “Obviously, I am a little bit biased because he is my opening partner [for Queensland] and a friend of mine, but he’s been there and done it. He has scored 184 for Australia.



“He has been in and out of the Australian team, and it allows you to grow, as I know from experience. It allows you to learn from experiences when you get the opportunity again. Whenever Rennie gets his chance ... I know he will be ready.” Renshaw has derived plenty from Khawaja, whether it’s cutting down on his cricket media consumption or choices of bats and shoes. In batting terms, Renshaw now has a lot more gears than the stodgy young player who ground out scores against South Africa, Pakistan and India. But he has retained an opener’s classical ability to recognise a tough session and play accordingly for his team, something Khawaja did well. Australia’s failure to do that in either innings of the Darwin Test is ultimately what cost Weatherald, and also has Marnus Labuschagne on the selection precipice. Alex Carey, a state teammate of Weatherald, said on Wednesday that he expected both the dropped opener and the team to rise from their poor showings in Darwin.



“It’s always difficult when someone is dropped from a team,” Carey said. “I flicked him a message yesterday and gave him my support, and look forward to him bouncing back in a big way in South Australian colours, and hopefully he can lead us to another Shield final, and also find his way back into the team. He’s only early 30s and has got a lot of class. “We’re a proud group of cricketers, and last week didn’t go to plan. We’ve reflected, we’ve talked about it, we always assess, have those conversations in real time as well, don’t have to wait until the end of the game to have those conversations. When this team has been challenged, we always find a way to bounce back in a big way.” Renshaw batting in the nets in Mackay. Getty Images A little bit of local knowledge won’t go astray here, however. Renshaw cuffed centuries in each of his two Sheffield Shield appearances for Queensland in Mackay. Personal development has also helped, whether in his home life or greater maturity around cricket teams.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket Why the Darwin disaster is a wake-up call for Australian cricket “I’ve got two kids now, so I can’t really say I’m a kid any more,” he quipped. “ I have a lot better understanding of my life and what’s important to me and how I’m going to go about things. So hopefully, it brings me a newfound sense of freedom. “I’ve evolved hugely as a person. As a cricketer, there’s things I look back on and go ‘geez, I was a terrible player’, but then I also look back and go ‘that would be nice to have’, so you definitely evolve.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Army joins search for missing Sydney bushwalker, 18
World.content:
The army has joined the search for missing Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper, a week after she failed to return from a trip to the Nattai National Park in the NSW Southern Highlands.

Close to 100 Australian Defence Force members joined the search on Wednesday, combining with other emergency services who have been looking for the 18-year-old since she went missing a week ago. Drones and helicopters have also been scouring the national park from the sky.

Lily Hooper, 18, is missing after going hiking in the Nattai National Park. NSW Police

Hooper was last seen leaving her home in Oakdale in Sydney’s south-west at 8am on Wednesday last week to go on a hike through the national park. Throughout the day, she remained in contact with her family, but they raised the alarm when she had not returned by 10pm.

Police found her Hyundai parked at the bottom of the challenging Bonnum Pic trail that night.

World.title: ‘I wish I got injured instead of him’: Brotherly love ahead of Trbojevic comeback
World.content:
Jake Trbojevic has paid tribute to brother Tom as he embarks on another comeback, saying most players in his position would have written off the year. Tom Trbojevic is a huge addition to a Manly side that remains a mathematical possibility of squeaking into the finals if they beat Newcastle at McDonald Jones Stadium on Saturday. The Sea Eagles haven’t won a game since their captain suffered his latest hamstring injury, in round 20. However, the fullback will be a welcome addition to a side that has lost halfback Joey Walsh to a fractured jaw. Another Trbojevic, youngest sibling Ben, also returns from injury. “I’ll be honest, it is tough, it’s really tough,” Jake Trbojevic said about playing without Tom.



“I’ve got a lot of respect for Tom, obviously being my brother and all that, but the way he goes about things – he is a true professional. “Everyone says that about people, but he genuinely is. Sometimes I wish it was me who got injured instead of him, because he puts in 10 times more work than anyone else to get his body right, and he’s just been very unlucky. Tom Trbojevic, Jake Trbojevic and Ben Trbojevic Getty Images “It’s very hard to see, particularly being his older brother. Not only that, selfishly I want him out on the field because he makes us better, you know? So, it is tough, but I’m happy for him that he’s very resilient and keeps working hard. These things don’t hold him back. “A lesser man would probably say, ‘You know what, I’ll just sit the year out and come back next year,’ but he’s fighting. He wants to be out there, he wants to lead this club, and that’s great.”



If Tom Trbojevic’s return is successful he could put himself into contention for Australia selection for the end-of-year World Cup. Much will depend on how he and Manly perform in coming weeks, although it’s unlikely the club will feature in the post-season. “There’s always a chance,” Jake Trbojevic said. “Tom wants to play for Manly, it doesn’t matter what’s on the line, he wants to be out there. He’s the captain of this club for a reason, and we love having him out there. The Northern Beaches loves having him out there. We’re better for it. Tom Trbojevic. Getty “So, it doesn’t matter what’s on the line—whether it’s finals or no finals—we want him out there, he wants to be out there, and he works extremely hard, so he deserves to be out there. We’re going to go out there, put in a great performance, and he’s going to lead us well. Hopefully, we can keep improving and turn this around.” Manly winger Jason Saab said Tom Trbojevic’s return would give the team a confidence boost.



“He’s a world-class player,” Saab said. “He’s had a tough run with injuries this year, but whenever he’s been fit and played the full game, he’s always had an impact. “We’re a better team when the Trbojevics are playing.” ‘Proud day for NRL’: Storm valued at $150m after sale goes through Adrian Proszenko



The Melbourne Storm has been valued at more than $150 million after the world’s second-biggest investment firm bought a majority share of the club. After an exhaustive process to find the right partner, the Storm has completed a landmark transaction with EQT, a Swedish firm with more than $333 billion in assets under management. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images The sale puts the Storm alongside Collingwood and the Brisbane Broncos as one of Australia’s top sporting franchises, just after the NRL brokered a $5.3 billion broadcast deal. Storm chair Matt Tripp – who remains a co-owner alongside Bart Campbell, Gerry Ryan, Tom Carroll and Brett Ralph – said the deal will elevate one of Australia’s top-performing sports clubs even higher.



“I’m really proud that a firm like EQT, who are a serious blue-chip investment company, has chosen us as the team in Australia that they want to invest in,” Tripp said. “That’s a credit to our people and the work that’s gone on over the last 27 years and the 13 years I’ve been involved as a club. “I’ve watched people work tirelessly at the Storm. Off the back of that, EQT recognised that and wanted to be part of that. It’s a really proud day for the club and the NRL more broadly. I think the NRL should be happy that a club has attracted the attention of a company like EQT.” The deal, which will result in EQT earning board seats, is subject to Australian Rugby League Commission approval. Tripp will remain chair, while other key positions will remain the same. “Absolutely status quo,” Tripp said. “I’m still the largest shareholder after EQT and I’m as committed as I’ve ever been. It wouldn’t matter if I owned one per cent of 100 per cent, I’m still as passionate and my desire to drive this club doesn’t waiver …



“These guys own the IMG Academy, which will be really beneficial for us. Related Article NRL 2026 Why a top-two finish by the NZ Warriors could cost NRL $3m “It’s one of the biggest academies in the world, they effectively groom and produce through their pathways academy in the US the best of the best in gridiron, basketball, baseball and the like. “In terms of sports science and everything that goes on that is best in class, we feel we can benefit from that and our new partners will assist us. “They are also huge investors in the AI space and data and hopefully some of that can be transformed into improving areas of the club.”



Latrell ‘a chance’ to make long-awaited return Christian Nicolussi Latrell Mitchell could make a long-awaited return for South Sydney this weekend, with coach Wayne Bennett admitting: “He’s a chance. He’ll still have to get through a couple of training sessions, but he’s some chance.” Bennett said last week Mitchell was likely to be held back for the penultimate week of the season – a round-26 clash against the Gold Coast Titans – but welcomed the prospect of having Mitchell back a week earlier, especially if his body could cope with a few opposed sessions. Latrell Mitchell could make his long-awaited return from injury against the Warriors on Saturday. Steven Siewert



Mitchell’s season looked over a few weeks ago, but he again trained away from the group on a soggy Monday morning as he overcomes a nerve issue in his lower back, which is causing problems down his leg and calf. The 29-year-old injured his back in an outstanding individual performance against Newcastle in round nine, then missed a week before aggravating it against the Dolphins during Magic Round. He hasn’t played since. Should Mitchell’s name be included on the team sheet on Tuesday, Bennett hinted he was unlikely to start, and would be eased into the game off the bench. Tallis Duncan has been playing at left centre in Mitchell’s absence, but is even more effective in the back row, which he will do when Mitchell returns. Latrell Mitchell stretches out at a wet Heffron Park on Monday morning. Steven Siewert



South Sydney need to win one of their remaining three games to cement a spot in the finals, and having a player such as Mitchell available would be a huge boost. The Rabbitohs host the high-flying New Zealand Warriors on Saturday at Accor Stadium, the Sydney Olympic Park venue where they have not lost a game this season. “I don’t know how far off he [Mitchell] is – the physios have a better understanding of that – but he was out there today doing strides … he’s a step closer again,” outside back Campbell Graham said on Monday. South Sydney are looking to continue their unbeaten run at Accor Stadium against the Warriors this weekend. Steven Siewert “Whenever he’s ready to go, we’ll more than welcome him back. We need to keep building as a group; we want to be a well-oiled machine by the time he’s back so he can come in and do his thing.



“He’s handled this situation well. And I’ve been there before where there’s no definite light at the end of the tunnel in terms of when you’ll be playing again. It’s a tough spot to be in. “But he’s full of energy, comes in every day smiling, and he’s great to have around the place.” Graham played his “veteran’s card” to join the rehab group on Monday as part of “load management” to avoid any fresh calf injuries. “I was stoked to get through the game last Friday,” he said. “I’m not out of the woods just yet, and I still have to manage my training loads.” No Red V lifeline as Sloan seeks Super League answers



Dan Walsh Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan says he has been “left in the dark” about the future of Castleford coach Ryan Carr, as St George Illawarra rule out extending an NRL lifeline to him and teammates Damien Cook and Mat Feagai if they look to back out of their Super League deals. Sloan conceded after the Dragons’ two-point win over Wests Tigers on Sunday that he has had second thoughts about his move to Castleford given the uncertainty around Carr’s position. Carr was a key reason Sloan signed a two-year deal with the club last month. Carr, who coached Sloan as an assistant and interim head coach at the Dragons, has been absent from Castleford for the past two weeks after the club launched an investigation into the 38-year-old with little detail or public explanation as to why. Castleford head of football Chris Chester has spoken to the Dragons trio and told them they remain in the club’s plans for next season regardless of Carr’s situation.



Loading St George Illawarra have moved on in their roster planning for 2027 and have privately conveyed that they do not have room for Sloan, Cook and Feagai in their salary cap after a significant recruitment and retention spree. “It definitely puts a big dent in things for me, I’ll be honest,” Sloan said. “Carry was a big reason why I signed over there. “Obviously we had a relationship here at the Dragons and I don’t really know the situation with him. We’ve been left in the dark. “I’m really excited to go over there if Carry is there, but I just don’t know if that’s going to be the case there. Hopefully I’ll find out soon what’s going on and they make a decision.



Dragons flyer Tyrell Sloan. Getty Images “I have thought about [trying to stay in the NRL], but I also have to keep playing good footy here to finish the season on a high.” Sloan, 24, has been playing with a new lease on life since Dean Young took charge of the Dragons, scoring eight tries in his past eight games. His time under predecessor Shane Flanagan was far less consistent with several demotions to reserve grade, and 18 months ago he was given permission to explore an early exit from the joint-venture. Immortal Andrew Johns has argued Sloan is “too good a player to be leaving the NRL at this age”, but the Indigenous All Stars representative acknowledged his form in previous years hadn’t left him with many options.



Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Twelve months ago, the Knights were heading for the wooden spoon. Holbrook must be coach of the year Malcolm Knox Journalist, author and columnist “I didn’t really have much [many options] in the NRL, and nothing really made sense, you know, to play in another jersey in the NRL,” Sloan said. “But Joey’s always been really good to me since I came into first grade and to be getting a fair rap from someone who has done everything in the game, I hold that in such respect. At the moment, I’ve got the Super League deal and at the end of it, I’ll only be 26. I’ve been in first grade since I was 18 so no matter what happens, I’d say I’ve got a lot of NRL left in me.”

World.title: Erin Patterson appeal LIVE: Mushroom killer seeks to challenge guilty verdict
World.content:
Crown prosecutor Jeremy McWilliams is now responding to Erin Patterson’s second appeal ground.

Specifically, her lawyers argue:

The cell tower evidence and evidence of death cap mushroom sightings in Loch and Outtrim posted to iNaturalist should not have been adduced in the applicant’s trial as the evidence was not (i) relevant or (ii) the probative value of that evidence was outweighed by its unfair prejudice and the admission of that evidence occasioned a substantial miscarriage of justice.

McWilliams has just gone through some of this contested evidence in detail as he argued it was used appropriately in Patterson’s trial.

“No such argument was made in relation to the iNaturalist evidence in the trial,” McWilliams said.

“The response is that this evidence was part of a collection of evidence which, taken together, demonstrated that the applicant had opportunity to deliberately source death cap mushrooms at a time close to the lunch, and on the prosecution case, did so.”

World.title: Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesRetail Opinion Retailers on the ropes as consumers all but close their wallets Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 19, 2026 — 3:50pm

August 19, 2026 — 3:50pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Punch-drunk retailers are attempting to lift themselves off the mat as consumers give them a dose of their own financial reality, keeping cash in their pockets. At the halfway mark of this year’s earnings season, the shareholder jury has spoken – the discretionary retail sector is in an unambiguous slump. Investors are just tapping out. The cyclical retail sector will eventually recover, but the trigger isn’t on the near-term horizon. Breville executes a tariff workaround. Meanwhile, consumers face a perfect storm of cost-of-living pressures thanks to interest rate rises, fuel prices, Middle East war-fuelled inflation and stalling real wages growth. Tumbling house prices and a lack of real estate turnover are the rotten cherry on top. To date, just one major listed retailer, Breville, has stopped short of flagging a performance warning – while releasing a result that included strong sales, albeit with earnings that were shy of pitch perfect.



The company’s financial performance had been buffeted by Donald Trump’s moveable feast on tariffs, which had pushed the appliance maker to move its manufacturing base out of China. Despite this disruption, the company posted a 1.7 per cent profit gain, thanks to what it described as the resilient premium consumer. Related Article Opinion

Global economy China’s breakneck plan to safeguard its future But the market is viewing any weakness with suspicion and isn’t taking any prisoners. Breville’s shares were hammered by about 5 per cent on Wednesday. Discretionary retail companies are watching their share prices tumble, as a conga line of chief executives admit that sales momentum has at best stalled, or at worst fallen off a cliff. Over the past five days, the consumer discretionary index has fallen more than 5 per cent compared with the ASX200, which is 1.7 per cent softer.



Sales from some of our most popular and resilient brands, including Peter Alexander, JB Hi-Fi and Temple & Webster, hit a wall either in the final quarter to June or in the six weeks since. And in the department store space, Myer has spoken of cost-of-living pressures driving down consumer sentiment, while David Jones’ move to further extend payment terms to suppliers speaks volumes about how it is travelling. JB Hi-Fi, which has been a consistent strong performer in the sector, flagged July total sales for its Australian stores were 1.8 per cent softer, with comparable sales growth falling 2.9 per cent. That is a significant reversal in growth from where it was a year ago. Myer has spoken of cost-of-living pressures driving down consumer sentiment. iStock Its other brand, The Good Guys, was 12 per cent lower in the early weeks of the new financial year, with comparable sales growth falling the same amount.



Homewares and furniture retailer Temple & Webster revealed a shock 62 per cent plunge in net profit after significant items, lowered its guidance, and warned revenue was down 13 per cent since the start of the 2027 financial year. It was the recent trading slide that spooked investors, who rewarded it with a near-18 per cent one-day share price collapse. It isn’t just that the consumers have all but closed their wallets, but one retailer after the next says that only discounts will entice shoppers to buy. So even if sales have held up, discounting is crunching margins and eating away at the profit line. It is difficult to find any near-term factors that will restore consumer confidence, given the odds are still in favour of another interest rate increase later this year and the turbulence playing out in the Middle East, which will keep a floor under petrol prices. The war will also feed into higher wholesale prices and further supply chain congestion. But how can retailers pass on these costs with higher consumer prices when shoppers refuse to transact unless goods are on sale?



Even those value investors looking for bargains might hold fire until retail stocks get even cheaper. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.
