World.title: Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Construction boss accused of plotting standover in secret sushi shop meeting with bikies Nick McKenzie Updated August 19, 2026 — 3:39pm ,first published 11:56am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A senior executive of Australian infrastructure giant BMD has been accused of secretly meeting violent members of a Melbourne bikie gang in a Brisbane sushi restaurant as part of a plot to threaten a CFMEU activist blamed for causing problems on an Albanese government-funded project. The revelations have prompted the Labor-backed CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby to issue a fresh call for government action to combat the “complete failure of the regulatory system”, while calling on companies with alleged links to bikie gangs and the underworld to “clean up” their backyards. BMD manager Robert Pickard has also been accused in a Queensland inquiry of attempting to cover up the incident after the CFMEU crane driver complained that the leader of a three-man Melbourne bikie crew had threatened to burn down his house and murder his family during a subsequent confrontation on the $350 million Centenary Bridge project. Counsel assisting the Queensland Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU, Eddy Gisonda KC, suggested on Wednesday afternoon that the terrifying stand-over incident occurred a short time after Pickard had met the bikie trio at a sushi shop a short stroll from the bridge redevelopment.



Related Article Building Bad ‘Burn your house and kill your kids’: Construction giant accused of using bikies But while being questioned by Gisonda, Pickard repeatedly denied allegations that he knew of or witnessed the alleged Comanchero gang standover on June 5, 2024. He also dismissed suggestions he had met the bikies at the sushi shop or coordinated the alleged standover with the owner of BMD’s security subcontractor, Melbourne company Host. Pickard’s denials came after Gisonda presented a detailed circumstantial case to back up his accusation that Pickard and BMD’s human resources chief, Steve Thomas, appeared to have played a key role in the suspected Comanchero standover of CFMEU-affiliated crane driver Cody Raymond, a man blamed for helping the construction union target BMD. Evidence aired by Gisonda before Commissioner Stuart Wood included receipts showing that one of the three bikies had purchased sushi just minutes after Pickard and Thomas had placed orders at the sushi shop. A short time after that, Pickard and Thomas can be seen on CCTV walking towards the Centenary Bridge project as they are trailed by three Comancheros and Melbourne businessman Gary Samuel, the BMD security subcontractor who was hired to counter an aggressive campaign by the CFMEU targeting BMD.



Pickard disagreed with Gisonda’s suggestion that he and Thomas had led the bikies to the work site at a distance to “to make sure the coast was clear” before Raymond was approached and threatened. Phone data presented by Gisonda also revealed repeated contact or attempted contact between Samuel and both Pickard and Thomas around the time Samuel was picking up the three Melbourne bikies from Brisbane airport, as well as just after what the barrister alleged was a secret rendezvous at the sushi outlet. During the hearing, Wood appeared to accept that Samuel had engineered the bikie standover in retaliation for the conduct of the CFMEU. “It makes sense for Mr Samuel to do this,” Wood suggested, referring to the use of the three feared bikie identities.



“It might be quite unlawful ... [but he had been] taking a knife to a gun fight and he wants to improve the tactics” in respect of BMD’s strategy, he said, to resist CFMEU pressure and in light of the indifference of state authorities to union conduct. “I am not saying it excuses him … But it gives a rational explanation for what he did,” Wood said of Samuel. Rob Pickard (right), General Manager, Queensland and Northern Territory, BMD Constructions is seen being questioned by Senior Counsel Assisting Eddy Gisonda KC (left) during the Commission of Inquiry. AAPIMAGE During the hearing, Wood also queried why BMD had told police in November 2024 that CCTV of the bikie incident was no longer available, given the company had provided the vision to Wood’s commission earlier this year. Wood also asked Gisonda to make inquiries about whether it was unlawful for a company or person to “deliberately or inadvertently mislead the police”. But Pickard dismissed the claim that he or BMD were party to a bikie threat plot or that Pickard had sought to “deflect” attention away from his own or Samuel’s role in allegedly coordinating the potentially criminal act.



Wednesday’s hearing will ultimately inform Wood as he weighs whether the circumstantial evidence gathered by Gisonda and the Queensland Police investigators assisting his inquiry is strong enough to allow Wood to make an adverse finding about Pickard or BMD’s involvement in the bikie plot. Gisonda opened the hearing on Wednesday by revealing that law enforcement agencies suspected the Comancheros of seeking to build a construction empire via front companies and by infiltrating union ranks. Queensland’s Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU has laid bare the involvement of the Comancheros in the construction industry. Getty Images He claimed police intelligence, including extensive phone data, indicated the Comanchero bikie gang had in early 2024 embarked on a concerted effort to do this in both Victoria and Queensland. According to Gisonda, this effort involved the now former Melbourne-based Comanchero boss Bemir Saracevic. Saracevic is the same bikie figure Gisonda identified as allegedly leading the standover of Raymond.



Gisonda also tabled union-backed enterprise bargaining agreements allegedly secured by Comanchero-linked building firms in Victoria, including an EBA signed off by the CFMEU administration last month and by the Australian Workers’ Union in 2025. A separate investigation by The Age has established that basic due diligence should have revealed to both unions that these firms had business links to the Comancheros: one had previously been refused a licence to operate by Victoria’s Labour Hire Authority, while both had clear links to the wife of Saracevic. Bemir Saracevic. Commission of Inquiry into the CFMEU In a statement, Crosby told this masthead that the EBA his union had recently granted a firm now alleged to be Comanchero-linked was intended to protect workers. The CFMEU administrator said it was up to government, and not the CFMEU, to prevent underworld infiltration. “The Administrator has called for a Fit and Proper Persons Test to be applied to participants in the construction industry. It’s time the industry was cleaned up. It’s time to stop blaming workers for the complete failure of the regulatory system. It’s not the job of the union to clean up the industry,” he said.



“We’ll clean up our backyard – it’s time for employers to clean up theirs.” Related Article Exclusive

Building Bad ‘Idiots in Victoria’ holding back CFMEU: Administrator blasts former union bosses, demands reform The Queensland hearing has also placed immense scrutiny on BMD, which is currently working on Victoria’s Eastern Freeway upgrade and other Big Build projects. In Sydney, it is working on the new international airport in Western Sydney. In July, the Crisafulli government in Queensland announced that BMD had won the contract to undertake early works for the new Brisbane Stadium Olympics venue. Asked by this masthead about the evidence heard at the commission suggesting BMD associated with underworld-linked figures in the alleged Centenary Bridge stand-over incident and whether BMD’s internal investigation into the matter was adequate, the company’s spokesperson said: “BMD has additional representatives to appear over the coming days and it would be premature for us to comment.”



The revelations at the Queensland inquiry give Australians a taste of what is likely to be unveiled at the promised and upcoming Victorian royal commission. Many of the key subjects discussed at this week’s hearings in Brisbane are from Melbourne and are variously entrenched in both Victoria’s underworld and its building sector. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I was a terrible player’: Renshaw bids to end opener roulette a decade after baby-faced debut
World.content:
Exclusive SportCricketAustralian cricket ‘I was a terrible player’: Renshaw bids to end opener roulette a decade after baby-faced debut Daniel Brettig Updated August 19, 2026 — 3:36pm ,first published August 19, 2026 — 9:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Matt Renshaw was still in something of a daze as he picked up his bags to resume life as a Test cricketer, a decade after being a “little baby” in the national team. Renshaw was at home in Brisbane with his wife Josie and their two young children on Monday night when the call came from selection chair George Bailey, telling him to get ready to join Australia as they try to overturn a surprise defeat by Bangladesh in Darwin. Matt Renshaw looks happy to be recalled to the Australian test team, especially given the match against Bangladesh is in Mackay, where he has made big scores in the past. Getty Images for Cricket Australia “I wasn’t really expecting it, so when the name came up on my phone I was quite surprised,” Renshaw, 30, told this masthead. “I look back at photos of myself 10 years ago and see a little baby playing Test cricket. It was pretty crazy, but hopefully this time getting the opportunity, I’ll be in a lot better mindset and a lot better frame.”



Despite being part of the 19-man training squad in Brisbane for six weeks leading up to the first Test, Renshaw had no inkling he was about to be returned to the top of the order, particularly given that Jake Weatherald had beaten him to a Cricket Australia contract. Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket The Test team’s five biggest problems: Is Lyon an automatic selection? “It was amazing preparation for me to get better,” he said. “That’s how I tried to use those couple of weeks, try to get better getting to face some of the best bowlers in the world three times a week was pretty cool. That’s all I saw it as, and fortunately I’m here now.” A host of players have been tried at the top of Australia’s batting order over the past decade, but none have been able to match Usman Khawaja, David Warner or more recently Travis Head. Renshaw, with an average of 36 over his first 10 Tests before sporadic appearance since, came closest. Renshaw now expects to open alongside Head, but he returns to the team with a raft of recent experience in other positions, not least in Bangladesh in a white-ball series earlier this year.



“I love opening,” Renshaw said. “I love the satisfaction that it brings when you perform after opening, but I feel like it’s held me in good stead doing it all around the order. “The white-ball stuff’s given me a different mindset and a little bit of freedom to express myself, to be able to bat and learn different things. Time down the middle order for Queensland gave me a bit more confidence as well.” Matt Renshaw with Pete Handscomb after his first Test hundred in January 2017. Getty It was against Bangladesh in 2017 that Renshaw ended his first stint in the Test side. Based on the numbers alone, it was a harsh call at the time, but having grown much as a person and a cricketer since, Renshaw feels well grounded for his chance to become Usman Khawaja’s long-term replacement at the top. “I know if Renshaw is picked that he is in the best space right now to have a crack at Australia again and be ready to score runs,” Khawaja said of Renshaw last summer. “Obviously, I am a little bit biased because he is my opening partner [for Queensland] and a friend of mine, but he’s been there and done it. He has scored 184 for Australia.



“He has been in and out of the Australian team, and it allows you to grow, as I know from experience. It allows you to learn from experiences when you get the opportunity again. Whenever Rennie gets his chance ... I know he will be ready.” Renshaw has derived plenty from Khawaja, whether it’s cutting down on his cricket media consumption or choices of bats and shoes. In batting terms, Renshaw now has a lot more gears than the stodgy young player who ground out scores against South Africa, Pakistan and India. But he has retained an opener’s classical ability to recognise a tough session and play accordingly for his team, something Khawaja did well. Australia’s failure to do that in either innings of the Darwin Test is ultimately what cost Weatherald, and also has Marnus Labuschagne on the selection precipice. Alex Carey, a state teammate of Weatherald, said on Wednesday that he expected both the dropped opener and the team to rise from their poor showings in Darwin.



“It’s always difficult when someone is dropped from a team,” Carey said. “I flicked him a message yesterday and gave him my support, and look forward to him bouncing back in a big way in South Australian colours, and hopefully he can lead us to another Shield final, and also find his way back into the team. He’s only early 30s and has got a lot of class. “We’re a proud group of cricketers, and last week didn’t go to plan. We’ve reflected, we’ve talked about it, we always assess, have those conversations in real time as well, don’t have to wait until the end of the game to have those conversations. When this team has been challenged, we always find a way to bounce back in a big way.” Renshaw batting in the nets in Mackay. Getty Images A little bit of local knowledge won’t go astray here, however. Renshaw cuffed centuries in each of his two Sheffield Shield appearances for Queensland in Mackay. Personal development has also helped, whether in his home life or greater maturity around cricket teams.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket Why the Darwin disaster is a wake-up call for Australian cricket “I’ve got two kids now, so I can’t really say I’m a kid any more,” he quipped. “ I have a lot better understanding of my life and what’s important to me and how I’m going to go about things. So hopefully, it brings me a newfound sense of freedom. “I’ve evolved hugely as a person. As a cricketer, there’s things I look back on and go ‘geez, I was a terrible player’, but then I also look back and go ‘that would be nice to have’, so you definitely evolve.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Damning report into fatal Mount Maunganui landslide shows tragedy was preventable
World.content:
Landslide risk at Mount Maunganui was found decades before fatal accident Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

A report into the fatal landslide at Mount Maunganui says information identifying a risk to life was received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left.

"The failure was not the fault of any one person; it was the failure of a system that enabled an identified risk to life to remain unowned, un-escalated and unmanaged," the report said.

Six people died in the landslide on 22 January 2026. They were Lisa Maclennan, Susan Knowles, Jacqualine Wheeler, Måns Loke Bernhardsson, Sharon Maccanico, and Max Furse-Kee.

The six victims of the Mt Maunganui landslide - Måns Loke Bernhardsson, 20, Lisa Maclennan, 50, Susan Knowles, 71, Sharon Maccanico, 15, Max Furse-Kee, 15, and Jacqualine Wheeler, 71. Supplied

The external review was commissioned by the Tauranga City Council in early February.

Retired high court judge Hon Paul Davison KSO KC, who wrote the report, said they had come to Mauao to do what thousands of New Zealanders do each summer - to camp in a spectacular setting beside the ocean beach and beneath a mountain of great beauty and cultural significance.

They trusted they would be safe and if any natural hazard risk arose, that they would be warned and protected.

"Nothing in this report should be allowed to obscure that," Davison said.

Watch the release of the findings below:

"The central conclusion of this review is sobering in its simplicity. This was not a hazard that was unknown, hidden, or beyond the reach of foresight.

"For more than two decades, one competent consultant after another identified the landslide hazard to the campground, located it on the very slope that failed, and explained - sometimes in stark terms - what the consequences of a landslide occurring could be.

"As long ago as 1999, Dr Laurie Richards warned that the siting of fragile holiday accommodation directly beneath these slopes was imprudent and that the risk to sleeping occupants was high."

The slip at Mauao, Mount Maunganui as seen from the air. Screengrab / Amy Till

He said in 2006 it went further, estimating that a debris flow of the kind that had happened before would place some 30 people in its path and kill 21.

The same warning and the same precisely-marked aerial photograph of the historic scarp was repeated "again and again" over the years that followed.

"And experience had repeatedly demonstrated that high levels of extended rainfall increased the likelihood of landslips occurring, and extremely high levels of extended heavy rainfall increased the risk of large scale landslides occurring."

Davison said in late 2023 and again in mid 2025, a Trigger Action Response Plan - which was an effective means of mitigating the risk - was recommended and not acted on.

"The knowledge was there. The means of reducing the risk of a landslide occurring was identified, available and relatively inexpensive to implement."

Floral tribute to the victims of the landslide. CHARLOTTE COOK / RNZ

He concluded that what was missing, was not knowledge, but an organisation able to hold, assess, and act on it.

"The geohazard sat at the administrative and legal boundary that exists between the mountain and the campground, and responsibility for landslide risk fell somewhere between the Tauranga City Council teams responsible for each."

Davison said no single person within the TCC organisation "owned it" and no system mandatorily required the risk to be recorded, escalated, or tracked.

"Reports identifying a risk to life were received, filed, discussed, forwarded - and then left."

Nick Monro

He said successive restructures dispersed the people who held the institutional memory and continuity of that invaluable knowledge was treated as expendable.

"Time and time again the recommended measures or controls were scoped out or simply not actioned."

Davison said on the morning of 22 January, these systematic flaws combined and were compounded.

"Warnings came early and from several directions."

This included from the intense rainfall, from the large slips already coming down around the mountain, from several smaller slips on the slope, and from muddy water streaming from the foot of the slope before it finally failed.

"The instinct to move people away from the toe of the slope was even voiced by some of those who observed these signs, but there was no plan against which to assess those warnings, no threshold criteria requiring action, and no training of staff enabling them to recognise observable signs which indicated an elevated risk of slope failure and no one charged with making a properly informed evacuation decision.

"The most consequential safety decision of that morning was left, by default, to the manager at the campground who have been given neither the tools nor the knowledge to make it.

"In my view, the criticism justly and appropriately lies with the organisation that left the campground manager and his staff so ill-equipped and unprepared to make the decisions that could have avoided this tragedy."

Tauranga mayor Mahé Drysdale speaks at a vigil a week after the landslide. Hayden Woodward

He said had a Trigger Action Response Plan of the kind been twice recommended, that morning would have looked very different.

"Such a plan would not have depended on anyone reading the slope correctly in the moment. Its rainfall trigger would likely have been engaged overnight, by rainfall that was the heaviest in some 20 years; and if not, independently by its second trigger - the prolific and very obvious discharge of muddy water from the toe of the slope, observable for several hours before the eventual slope failure - should have required the same response."

He said each trigger on their own would have called for at least the precautionary evacuation and exclusion of the campsites.

"Had those areas been evacuated and kept clear, as such a plan would have required, the people who lost their lives would not have been within the path of the landslide when the slope failed.

"The loss of life could have in all likelihood been averted."

Davison said it was important to be clear that the review did not find that any individual did anything intentionally wrong, or that any one or more persons' acts or omissions caused these deaths.

He also did not find that the removal of trees in 2019 caused the landslide and makes no findings as to civil, criminal, or disciplinary liability.

Emergency Management Minister reacts to Mount landslide report Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

What it did find, he said, was that the tragedy was preventable.

"I do not mean by that that anyone could have known that this slope would fail at this moment, on this particular morning - no one could.

"I mean something more deeply troubling; that the hazard was known, that an effective and inexpensive means of managing the risk it posed had twice been recommended, and that the council had every opportunity to put it in place.

"What was required was not extraordinary foresight."

Davison said the recommendations he's made are directed to building a single accountable ownership of every risk to life.

"Mauao is a revered taonga, a sacred maunga, a place of belonging, of healing, and of inspiration for the people of Tauranga Moana, and for many people privileged to visit it and who hold and treat it with respect.

"It will always be so. But the events of 22 January 2026 have shown, at the most heartbreaking cost, that reverence for the mountain and responsibility for those who climb it or gather at its foot must go hand in hand.

"While the law draws a boundary between the reserve and the campground, the mountain recognises no such line, and neither does the landslide risk that lies within its slopes."

He said if the recommendations are acted upon, it will materially reduce the chance of such a tragedy ever occurring again.

Speaking after the report's release, police said the investigation into the landslide was ongoing.

World.title: Riding horse to work 'ticked off bucket-list goal', police officer says
World.content:
A police officer who rode a horse named Kitty to work says he wanted to "tick off a bucket-list goal", and had no idea how much attention his unusual mode of transport would attract.

RNZ earlier reported that a police officer rode his horse into work at the Christchurch Central Police Station in April.

It's understood the horse caught the attention of fellow staff after it was stationed at the Christchurch Central Police Station alongside more conventional transport options, such as bicycles and scooters.

Christchurch metro area commander Superintendent Lane Todd earlier said the horse was "saddled up with the bicycles for about an hour".

"This is nay an approved vehicle that can be parked onsite, and the officer was told to hold his horses, he did not have free rein to keep the horse there. It has since been scratched and sent home."

The officer wrote about his trip to work in the latest Police News magazine saying they "wanted to clear some stuff up".

"My horse, Kitty, is a 15-year-old Hanoverian mare and my main working horse when I go mustering.

"Riding her into work was something I'd talked about for more than a year."

The officer said before riding the horse to work he made sure everyone who needed to know was aware of his plans, including the district commander and building management team.

"I even did a health and safety plan as per Police policy and went through relevant legislation and bylaws to make sure what I was doing was legal.

"We left before dawn and arrived in the city just before 6am. For me, riding a horse is nothing unusual. I had no idea how much attention it would attract."

The officer said a couple of hours into his shift "my phone was off the charts".

"Bosses told me I hadn't done anything wrong, but they didn't want media attention during pay round. I was asked to take Kitty home. I did so without argument and the ride back turned into a memorable experience in itself.

"What stood out for me was the reaction from the public and colleagues. People stopped to chat, ask questions and take photos. Lots of staff told me it brightened their day, and some even said it was a career highlight."

The officer said there was "never any ulterior motive or protest".

"I genuinely just wanted to tick off a bucket-list goal and hopefully bring a smile to a few faces.

"In the end, no wrongdoing was found, Kitty returned to living her life back in the hills and I was reminded how much goodwill there is towards police when people get to see us simply as fellow Kiwis."

The officer's name was withheld.

World.title: Auckland seaside village redevelopment seeks fast-track approval
World.content:
A contentious plan to re-develop a seaside village on Auckland's North Shore has been referred to the fast-track approvals process, despite community opposition.

Infrastructure Minister Chris Bishop accepted Peninsula Capital's 'Devonport Lanes' application on Tuesday, and their proposal would now be reviewed by a panel of experts.

But some locals - including the Devonport Heritage group - raised concerns at a public meeting in June about buildings towering up to six storeys above the suburb's heritage main street and blocking views of the Takarunga Maunga.

The group staged a protest earlier this month, raising red balloons 27 metres into the air to show how high eight-storey buildings would rise in Devonport village.

Peninsula Capital managing director Mark Hiddleston confirmed the 50-room hotel, four residential apartment buildings and shopping precinct the company wanted to construct would be four to eight storeys high.

"It's not that it hasn't been considered. We knew it would be contentious.

"Height allows this development to take place, to ensure that we can provide the restoration, and ultimately we're trying to bring vibrancy back to Devonport village."

Hiddleston said Peninsula Capital had worked with Heritage NZ and Auckland Council's heritage experts on the plans.

"This has always been about much more than developing a site. It's about bringing more people into Devonport, restoring and finding new uses for some really important heritage buildings, and helping make sure the town centre has a strong future.

"Devonport is a fantastic place, but its town centre needs people in it, and its beautiful heritage buildings need investment, restoration and ongoing care. More people living here means more people using the shops, cafés, restaurants and services every day. We want to create somewhere people genuinely want to live, stay and spend time, while keeping the things that make Devonport Devonport."

He acknowledged that traffic on Lake Road - the only road into Devonport - was an issue that needed consideration.

"That's why the village is an appropriate place to put more density and more intensification because you've got the ferry, a great piece of infrastructure, and one of Auckland's best-used facilities, right there.

"Lake Road and the traffic woes need to be addressed, but I don't think we're going to make that problem worse."

Devonport heritage chair Margot McRae comparing planned development with the current downtown Devonport streetscape. RNZ / Jessica Hopkins

But Devonport Heritage chair Margot McRae said that, unlike getting a resource consent through the local council, the fast-track process allowed Peninsula Capital to block out dissenting opinions.

"Three years ago they [Peninsula] wanted to work with us, they wanted to consult us, and they saw Devonport Heritage as a key stakeholder. But once fast-track came along, they didn't need to meet us any more.

"That's why I'm saying to them, please invite us to be part of the process."

Hiddleston said that while everyone in the community's opinions were relevant, Devonport Heritage's concerns had already been voiced through the media.

"Fast track is a legitimate process. Three years ago it didn't exist, and we believe it's an appropriate process to run through.

"The panel of experts will consider heritage as we have."

World.title: Politicians weigh in after revelations of Health NZ hiring crackdown
World.content:
The Health Minister insists he never accepted a policy by senior health officials to keep tight controls on hiring frontline health staff.

But the Greens have accused Simeon Brown of "weaponising" a bureaucratic process to save costs in the health system.

Politicians have weighed in following RNZ's revelations of the hiring controls at Health New Zealand.

In a briefing to Brown in March last year, then health commissioner Professor Lester Levy and interim chief executive Dr Dale Bramley said tight controls on recruitment were crucial to meeting last year's budget, and hiring frontline workers required the sign off of the deputy chief executive.

An internal document also revealed that regional panels had been set up in June 2024 to sign off all hiring decisions, while there was a freeze on hiring non-clinical roles.

The documents were released under the Official Information Act to the Public Service Association (PSA), which says the policy led to crucial roles being left vacant for months, and patients suffering as a result.

Brown hit out at the PSA on Wednesday, saying he never accepted the policy, and had made a speech last March stating the need for regional decision-making.

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons. Supplied

"It doesn't surprise me that the PSA union, which is literally campaigning for a change of government, is pulling up a document from the beginning of last year when I first became the minister of health."

He said there had been a "huge amount of change" since the briefing document last year was provided to him.

"Since then, we've got a new board, a new CE. We've put in place devolution, which is devolving decision-making back down to regions and districts so that these local decisions are made closer to home so that recruitment can be sped up."

Brown said he sent a letter of expectation to the agency in November last year, reiterating the need to devolve decision-making to regions and speed up hiring.

"It's a big bureaucracy that was set up by the previous government during the middle of a pandemic. We've been very clear about our expectations that these decisions need to be made closer to the regions and the districts."

When asked whether Health NZ had continued the policy after his March speech, or made the hiring changes quickly enough, Brown said he wants the agency to "move faster to speed up recruitment".

PSA national secretary Fleur Fitzsimons said the policy had meant crucial roles were kept vacant for months, including six months to hire three neo-natal nurses, and stroke patients suffering from a lack of services due to under-staffing.

When asked about patients, Brown did not directly say whether people had suffered as a result of hiring lags, adding he was intent on fixing a "really bureaucratic machine".

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

But Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said the documents revealed that Te Whatu Ora deliberately delayed filling clinical roles to save money.

"The PSA provided damning evidence that the minister of health has knowingly weaponised the bureaucracy to slow the recruitment of health workers as a cost saving measure."

The government had consistently said it would not cut front line services to balance the budget, Davidson said, but the union's report had revealed "reckless cuts to funding".

"It's appalling to see that more than three quarters of staff have had to wait more than a month to get approval to fill a vacancy, including delays to staff three neo-natal intensive care unit nurses at Capital, Coast and Hutt Valley hospitals."

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins said it was becoming clear the National government was forcing the health system to breaking point.

"The hiring freeze they've had across the country, stopping vacancies being filled is causing real harm to New Zealanders. It's meaning that Kiwis are not getting the health care that they are entitled to under our health system."

A Health NZ spokesperson has previously said that it has now changed its hiring processes, and the four regional recruitment panels for budgeted staff no longer existed.

World.title: Former Silver Ferns' skipper Ameliaranne Ekenasio says Australia move was easy decision
World.content:
Faced with the possibility of an enforced early retirement, former Silver Ferns' captain Ameliaranne Ekenasio says the decision to play in the Australian netball league became an easy one.

Ekenasio has extended her career by signing with the West Coast Fever in the Australian netball league for 2027.

Ekenasio is the first of several new Kiwi players expected to be announced in the coming days to feature in next year's Suncorp Super Netball (SSN) league.

Top New Zealand players have been forced to look overseas, with Netball NZ not able to provide any assurances there will be an elite domestic competition next year.

Timing and circumstances have previously denied Ekenasio from fulfilling a long-held dream of competing in the Australian league.

But with no certainty around the direction of New Zealand's domestic competition for next year, the decision was made easier for the 35-year-old when the Fever came calling.

With her family to consider, Ekenasio said she had to work through some logistics with the Fever but knowing her husband and two children will move over to Perth sealed her decision.

Ekenasio co-captained the Pulse this year, but the ANZ Premiership franchises are unable to offer any contracts to players at this point in time.

Ameliaranne Ekenasio co-captained the Pulse this year. Marty Melville / www.photosport.nz

The silky long-range shooter said an early retirement was on the cards if she didn't get a contract in the SSN.

"I didn't have anything here, nobody has anything here in New Zealand so it just made total sense. I was definitely thinking that if I didn't have any opportunities in Australia, and if there was no league here in New Zealand, I would have to retire.

"That was quite confronting to think about you know, that I potentially would have had to retire if I didn't have a chance to play anymore."

Now in the twilight of her career, Ekenasio thought the opportunity might have passed her by.

"It always has been a dream of mine to go over and play in Suncorp, that was the main driver and to play with such an incredible team like the Fever, to have the opportunity, that was the massive draw card," Ekenasio said.

"And there's been so many restraints on us in the past in being able to do it, plus I've got a family so it's not as easy to just move over at the drop of a hat but we're at the right time in our family life that we can pack up and move."

Netball New Zealand relaxed its eligibility rules last year, making it much easier for players to be granted exemptions to play in Australia while still being able to play for the Silver Ferns.

The national body recently scrapped any restrictions around New Zealand players competing overseas, given it could not provide any guarantees that there will be an elite domestic competition next year.

Ekenasio said it was sad watching the potential demise of the ANZ Premiership, which would affect many of her former team-mates.

"I'm just devastated for all of the girls, I am so heartbroken for netball in New Zealand.

"We are the leading [women's] sport in New Zealand and I know we're competing with so many other sports now, but to see the sport go downhill. We play it because we love it but it is also a job and lots of us need to put food on the table and that's just the reality of it.

"I really feel for the players and without a professional league how do we expect girls who are playing at grassroots and that's the thing - netball courts are absolutely jam-packed every Saturday so it just doesn't make sense. How will they see the stepping stones to become a Silver Fern and to be great if they cannot see girls playing professionally week in week out?"

Current Silver Ferns' captain Karin Burger has confirmed she is staying on for a second SSN season at the Sunshine Coast Lightning.

Midcourter Maddy Gordon has advised the Queensland Firebirds that she will be accepting an offer elsewhere and Silver Ferns' shooter Grace Nweke is leaving the NSW Swifts after two seasons for another Australian club yet to be announced.

Kate Heffernan is expected to stay at the Premiership winning Adelaide Thunderbirds for 2027, and defender Kelly Jackson at the Queensland Firebirds for a second season.

Current Silver Ferns' captain Karin Burger is staying on for a second SSN season at the Sunshine Coast Lightning. Simon Stacpoole / Photosport

But the reality is of the 60 players contracted across the six ANZ Premiership teams this year, the majority won't get a contract in Australia or the UK league.

Ekenasio said she felt for those players.

"I have lots of friends who will be staying in New Zealand who won't have the opportunity to come over to Australia to play and that is really hard. I put myself in their shoes and couldn't imagine being like a budding Silver Fern on the brink of making it and having no idea if you've got a job next year or whether it will take you to the next level.

"I'm really hopeful that something pulls through for them, so trying to remain positive but at the same time just really disheartened by the lack of it moving forward. The uncertainty has been really hard for all of us, especially all of us who have poured our entire lives into netball, it's heartbreaking."

Ekenasio elected to step away from the Silver Ferns last year, saying she needed a break "for my mind, body and spirit".

Born in Australia, Ekenasio began her elite domestic career in the former trans-Tasman ANZ Championship playing for the Queensland Firebirds.

Searching for more court time, Ekenasio moved to New Zealand to join the Pulse in 2015 and dual citizenship saw her fast-tracked into the Silver Ferns.

During her 79-Test career she claimed Constellation Cup success and was a vital member of the Silver Ferns' 2019 Netball World Cup-winning side.

Ekenasio said she was immensely proud watching the Silver Ferns win gold at the recent Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

World.title: Christopher Luxon denies 'ridiculous' accusation by Labour's Chris Hipkins
World.content:
Christopher Luxon has labelled Labour's Chris Hipkins "ridiculous" for accusing him of insulting his own National Party backbenchers as "no better than a bunch of Air New Zealand middle managers".

"It's not something I would say," Luxon told reporters at Parliament on Wednesday.

Hipkins made the claim on Tuesday afternoon during a fiery debate about the sacking of Chris Penk from Cabinet, telling MPs that Luxon had badmouthed his caucus colleagues to a group of businesspeople in Auckland.

"I'm not sure who should be more offended by that: the National Party backbench or the middle managers at Air New Zealand, who, frankly, deserve a hell of a lot more respect than that," Hipkins said.

Asked for more details on Wednesday, Hipkins said he was told about the exchange by an Auckland businessperson "a couple of years ago" but did not have any proof.

"I'm taking that person at their word," Hipkins said.

Luxon told reporters that the Labour leader was just trying to create a side-show and distraction.

"That's a ridiculous thing from Chris Hipkins," Luxon said.

"He's under pressure because he wants to level nine new taxes on New Zealanders. It's not something I would say."

Luxon said the media should instead be focusing on Labour's proposed capital gains tax and its "unfunded promises".

"I get it. [Hipkins] wants to make the election about me. I want to make this election about taxes and New Zealanders."

Hipkins sought to revive the National Party's recent failed coup during Parliament's Question Time on Wednesday afternoon, questioning Luxon over when he first learnt that his colleagues wanted to replace him.

"We've dealt with it. We're moving on," Luxon said.

In an act which prompted jeers from the opposition, National minister Chris Bishop twice leapt to his feet to try stop the question line, arguing that it related to a "party political matter", not the prime ministership.

Hipkins was ultimately allowed to ask whether "any other minister in his government indicate that he should stand down as prime minister during the last two weeks".

Luxon responded: "Chris Penk was the only person to challenge for the leadership. He was working for himself."

Hipkins also asked whether Luxon agreed with New Zealand First leader Winston Peters' description of National MPs as "inexperienced, egotistical and self-obsessed".

World.title: No 'silver bullet' for cutting high power bills - Energy Minister
World.content:
The Energy Minister says there's "no silver bullet" for reducing power bills.

The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) has produced a discussion document - asking whether legislative changes are needed to make the sector more efficient and affordable.

Energy MInister Simeon Brown said he was seeking advice from gentailers and the Electricity Authority on tackling higher power bills.

Government sets sights on power network companies Morning Report Download MP3 8m

But he would not tell Morning Report who had answered him so far.

"It's critical we get this right," he said.

However, there was "no silver bullet" to tackle the problem.

Instead, he said that only focusing on wholesale prices missed one of the biggest drivers of rising bills - line companies.

Network charges which cover things like substations, poles and wires make up a quarter of household bills and accounted for two-thirds of recent price increases.

"We also have to focus on all of the things which are driving up power bills for customers. As I said, wholesale prices are reduced, we expect the big companies to pass that on to customers."

He said the document suggested a price-quality pass for all line companies to "ensure customers get a fair deal" and to "put downward pressure for consumers to make sure they're getting a fair deal".

He said the Commerce Commission did not have the powers it needed to regulate the "natural monopolies" lines companies represented.

Brown also called for ringfencing money from power bills like water companies do to ensure the money goes back into the infrastructure people pay to use.

In a media statement Brown said distribution companies needed to come to the affordability party.

"There are 28 Electricity Distribution Businesses (EDBs) in New Zealand, responsible for local infrastructure like power lines, poles and substations. Some EDBs are subject to price-quality regulation in which the Commerce Commission sets their maximum revenue and minimum service standards.

"Regulated revenues were last set in 2024 when interest rates had risen substantially following record inflation. Unfortunately, due to the high interest rates at that time, consumers are paying right now for that excess, on top of the cost of preparing networks for the greater electrification that is under way, and the increased demand that is coming."

The minister said an affordable electricity system was one of the government's priorities.

"The discussion document released by MBIE today sets out options to strengthen the performance of EDBs so they can provide reliable and affordable services to consumers while supporting increased electrification and innovation."

The three key areas the government was aiming to take further action regarding EDBs were:

Collaboration and standardisation

More responsive economic regulation

Stronger governance and accountability

"The cost of electricity and potential for rising bills is front of mind for New Zealand households and businesses. I expect the sector to play its part in improving affordability for Kiwis by boosting efficiency, including through greater collaboration and standardisation," Brown said.

"Positive work is underway, but more change is needed to make the system more affordable for households and businesses."

Commerce and Consumer Affairs Minister Cameron Brewer said the scale of investment required for New Zealand's energy transition raises questions about whether the current arrangements will continue to deliver the best outcomes for consumers in the future.

World.title: Govt considers u-turn on climate change in school curriculum
World.content:
The government is reviewing the deletion of climate change from the subjects children will study at primary school and the first years of secondary, while claiming it was never really cut in the first place.

The topic was in draft Science and Social Sciences curriculums for students in Years 0-10 but was axed from the final versions published last week.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the topic was still in the curriculum even if it was not explicitly mentioned.

"Climate change already is in the curriculum," she said.

"For some reason the writers didn't use the word 'climate change' or it didn't end up in the final document so I've instructed the ministry to go back and just talk to the experts, climate change experts, to make sure we're actually using the term in the areas where we are talking about climate change, so they're going back and doing a review of that."

Stanford said climate change was included when she looked at the final version of the curriculums before they were published.

"When I read through the very final one, the day before it went out, I could see that climate change was included. It's just about putting the word back in," she said.

Stanford said she did not know why the term was deleted as she was not involved in writing the curriculum and it was not her decision.

She said the topic was in the draft senior secondary school curriculum.

'Not connected in a coherent way'

But University of Waikato education professor Chris Eames said it was not accurate to claim climate change was in the curriculums published last week even if the term was not explicitly used.

"Although various aspects that contribute to or are impacts of climate change are certainly present, they are not connected in a coherent way, and they are certainly not attributed to human activity," he said.

"This means that learning and teaching about climate change is likely to remain fragmented and not lead to student understanding about how we can address climate change, which is absolutely what is needed for them to learn so that when they can address it, they have the abilities to do so."

Eames said the ministry did not consult any of the climate education experts he knew and he wondered who advised it on the climate change content.

On Monday evening Prime Minister Christopher Luxon responded to a question about the place of climate change science in schools by saying the government had to focus first on maths, reading and attendance.

World.title: Ikitau back in fray as Wallabies eye Argentina tour
World.content:
Les Kiss has resisted throwing any curveballs ahead of the Wallabies' tour of Argentina, with a fit Len Ikitau the only addition to the squad that produced wins in his first two Tests as coach.

Ikitau (ankle), the 2025 Wallabies player of the year, had minor surgery and missed the recent victories against Japan in Osaka and Townsville.

He has effectively replaced unlucky fullback Jock Campbell, who impressed in the number 15 jersey against Ireland before injuries elsewhere saw him employed as a play-making bench option against France.

With Tom Wright locked in at fullback, Campbell, who was named the Queensland Reds' best player at this week's end-of-season awards, was replaced by Ben Donaldson as the fullback or fly half bench cover for the next three Tests.

Les Kiss seeking pride The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Centre Josh Flook has also been left out while Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii (hamstring) will also return after missing Saturday's Townsville Test, creating a log-jam of midfield options against the world number seven Pumas.

Winger Max Jorgensen has been included despite coming off with a sore chest on Saturday, while code-hopper Zac Lomax remains on the injury list and unavailable for selection.

Lock Miles Amatosero, unavailable for the first Test as part of a three-game suspension for a red card earned in Osaka, was also not considered for selection.

Kiss, who tested new combinations in the pack and centres in his first two games in charge, has otherwise played a straight bat ahead of what will be sterner tests in San Salvador de Jujuy and Mendoza on August 30 and September 6.

"As coaches, we've looked to maintain consistency in selection, with the bulk of this squad having laid a solid foundation over the past few weeks through their hard work and connection on and off the field," he said.

"Touring Argentina presents another tough challenge for us as a new group, and it's one that we know will require us to go to another level as we continue to look to build and develop our game."

Where Kiss selects Suaalii will be telling after Isaac Henry's strong running and second-phase play at outside centre caught the eye in Townsville.

Hunter Paisami has also impressed at number 12 in Ikitau's absence, leading to questions post-match about where Suaalii fits in the picture.

There is a push for former NRL star Suaalii to move to the wing to ensure more involvement and better harness his aerial ability.

Kiss, who replaced Joe Schmidt ahead of next year's home Rugby World Cup, said before his first Test in charge that he was "persisting at number 13 with him at this stage, but I know that he can go to fullback and wing, and that's important to acknowledge as well".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

But Campbell and Flook's exclusion from this squad hints that Kiss is now considering a Suaalii switch.

Zane Nonggorr (calf) remains sidelined, with Massimo De Lutiis set for his first full Wallabies tour after arriving late into Osaka and debuting in Townsville.

Wright will notch 50 Test caps if he plays in both Tests.

The squad will assemble in Sydney on Saturday, before departing for Buenos Aires on Sunday.

WALLABIES SQUAD: Allan Alaalatoa, Angus Bell, Charlie Cale, Josh Canham, Massimo de Lutiis, Tom Hooper, Isaac Kailea, Fraser McReight, Josh Nasser, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Billy Pollard, Aidan Ross, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Lachlan Shaw , Carlo Tizzano, Taniela Tupou, Rob Valetini, Jeremy Williams, Harry Wilson (c), Filipo Daugunu, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Isaac Henry, Len Ikitau, Max Jorgensen, Ryan Lonergan, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Hunter Paisami, Dylan Pietsch, Harry Potter, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Kalani Thomas, Tom Wright.

AAP

World.title: Germany star says neurological issue behind two collapses in a week
World.content:
Bayern Munich midfielder Jamal Musiala has revealed a neurological issue but says he is doing well despite collapsing during a preseason game for the second time in a week.

The 23-year-old Germany international went down shortly after entering Wednesday's (AEST) friendly as a substitute in the second half. Players from both teams made a circle around Musiala as he received medical treatment. He was then helped as he walked off the pitch.

Musiala had collapsed Sunday (AEST) during a friendly against Leipzig. German news agency DPA reported he had left the field on his own but still appeared dazed.

After Wednesday's game, Musiala posted a message on his Instagram account, explaining that he had been diagnosed with temporary "but easily treatable absence seizures" caused by a neurological problem.

"These can lead to the moments that happened recently, such as against Leipzig or even now in Heidenheim," Musiala wrote.

Bayern, in its report on Wednesday's game, only said of the incident: "There was a setback when Jamal Musiala had to be subbed off with a knock minutes after coming on."

Jamal Musiala was held up by teammate Ismael Saibari (left) after fainting during Bayern's friendly against RB Leipzig. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Musiala said he was "very optimistic" and was receiving excellent medical treatment.

"The important thing is that there is no additional health risk," he wrote.

"In close coordination and regular communication with experts, it has been my personal wish to face the challenge and, with the endorsement of the neurological specialists, to devote myself to what helps me most in recovery: to simply live my everyday life and keep up with my passion of playing football," Musiala added.

Bundesliga champion Bayern faces Borussia Dortmund on Sunday AEST in the German Supercup, the traditional curtain-raiser for the season.

World.title: Irankunda says Hanson's monoculture comments upset team during World Cup
World.content:
Socceroos star winger Nestory Irankunda says One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's comments on multiculturalism upset many of the players during the recent World Cup.

The Australian team was competing at the tournament in North America in June when Ms Hanson made a speech at the National Press Club saying Australia should end its policy of multiculturalism in favour of a monoculture.

"It really did upset me and it upset a lot of the other boys to see things and hear things like that," Irankunda said.

" I felt a bit emotional but then tried to forget about it. "

Irankunda, who is one of several Socceroos players from a refugee background, told 702 ABC Sydney while he tried to stay off social media it was hard to avoid the senator's comments.

Loading...

"There can be some people who do the wrong thing but that doesn't mean that's all of us," he said.

"There's people like me, and Awer [Mabil], Mohamed Touré that go out there. There's a lot of boys like us that go out there and do the right thing.

"I don't like how they try and put us in the whole same category as the other people who do bad."

Irankunda was born in a refugee camp in Tanzania in 2006 to Burundian parents who fled the nation's civil war. He came to Australia when he was three months old.

Irankunda was speaking with presenter Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney just days after moving from English Championship club Watford to Portuguese side Sporting CP for an undisclosed fee reported to be in the region of $26 million.

The footballer said he probably wouldn't like to speak with the One Nation senator as he was still upset by the comments and "some of the things she said in the past".

"I'm not someone that likes to jump into controversial things or this political stuff. But I mean, you know, you never know," Irankunda said.

"One day I could be on the phone with her or sitting in an office chatting to her. So I mean … we'll see what happens."

Pauline Hanson's speech at the National Press Club included a call to end Australia's decades-old policy of multiculturalism. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

After her press club speech, Hanson said the Socceroos represented her vision of a monocultural Australia.

"People from different background and cultures and nations all wearing the green and gold and representing one nation under one flag and succeeding under the same set of rules," Hanson said in the Senate in June.

Socceroo Awer Mabil addressed the monoculture debate when he returned in July from the tournament, declaring his team was not distracted and that it was "all bullshit" to suggest Australia was not a multicultural society.

Australian team destined to 'go far'

Irankunda said despite the Round of 32 loss to Egypt, the Socceroos had youth on their side and could go further into the tournament.

"You can see now with the likes of Lucas Herrington, Ali [Alessandro] Circati, Jordy Bos, you know, Mohamed Touré, all these names, all these young boys coming through, including myself," Irankunda said.

"There's still a lot of talent coming through in Australia right now.

"Only time will tell how far we can go. But I feel like in my heart that we can go pretty far."

World.title: 'Embarassed and ashamed': Swans CEO explains decision to ban players
World.content:
The Sydney Swans say their willingness to "torpedo" their AFL season by suspending five star players proves how committed they are to upholding standards at the club.

The Swans suspended Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Isaac Heeney, James Jordon and Chad Warner for the remainder of the 2026 AFL season over an alleged incident at a Melbourne hotel in the early hours of Monday morning.

At least five players were linked to an ongoing Victoria Police investigation into an alleged sexual assault at the Pullman Hotel, where the Swans were staying after their win over Essendon on Sunday night.

It is not suggested that any of the players are being accused of sexual assault and none of the banned players have been formally interviewed by police, according to the club, or charged.

Telstra has spoken out saying they were "deeply concerned by what's been reported" and respected that the matter was currently being investigated by police.

"Players assisting police with their investigation who are also Telstra ambassadors are not participating in any ambassador activity while the investigation is ongoing," a Telstra spokesperson said.

"We will review their ambassador arrangements once the investigation is complete and will provide an update at that time."

It is understood that Heeney and Warner have both been Telstra ambassadors.

Swans sponsors QBE came out in support of the club's actions.

"QBE acknowledges the seriousness of the allegations that have been reported," a spokesperson said today.

"We have no tolerance for conduct that compromises the safety, dignity or wellbeing of others and we support the club's position in condemning all forms of abuse and disrespectful behaviour towards women.

"Given there is an active police investigation it would be inappropriate for us to comment any further."

Another club sponsor, realestate.com.au, also responded, saying they were "deeply concerned about the serious allegations involving several Sydney Swans players".

"We are aware there are investigations currently being conducted by the relevant authorities and await the findings of those investigations," a company spokesperson said.

Swans sanctions solely for breaches of club standards

(Clockwise from top left) James Jordon, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner and Isaac Heeney have been stood down. (ABC News/Getty Images)

Swans chairman Andrew Pridham and chief executive Matthew Pavlich have stressed the decision to ban the players is solely related to breaches of the club's standards and expected behaviour.

"Hopefully people can see how seriously we've taken this matter," Pridham said.

"We're very proud of our culture we've built over many years at the club. We get more right than we get wrong. Clearly this is a very sad day for us and for everybody involved.

Swans chief executive Matthew Pavlich (left) and chairman Andrew Pridham. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

"I know the five players involved, they're extremely remorseful for their actions in breaching the club's standards, and I think the sanction we've imposed and the impact that will have on our football season is clear for all to see.

"It's very important to note the football outcome was not a consideration of the board."

Sydney's sanctions came after the club conducted interviews with the players linked to the Melbourne incident off-site with their lawyers present. Sydney's board met on Tuesday night to discuss club-imposed sanctions.

Focus should not be on 'football consequences' AFLW star turned broadcaster Kate McCarthy calls out members of the media focusing on how a police investigation linked to Sydney Swans players could affect the team's finals chances.

The bans handed to the players, according to the club bosses, relate to their decision to continue drinking late into the night and bring women back to the hotel.

Pavlich said it fell "a long way short of what we expect of our players", and Pridham added that their actions left the club with no choice but to impose a heavy sanction.

"They shouldn't have been in that situation," Pridham said.

"The only way we can deal with it is to put our foot down incredibly hard, which we've done. To effectively torpedo our season by making a decision such as this tells you how seriously we're taking this."

The AFL has backed the team's sanctions and the Swans say their decision is independent of an ongoing Victoria Police investigation.

The rest of the Swans will prepare for North Melbourne on Sunday and then a finals campaign. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The players' ban includes this Sunday's home-and-away finale against North Melbourne and any finals matches the Swans will play afterwards.

Pavlich said the club was "deeply embarrassed and ashamed", stressing they were "deeply concerned" about the welfare and wellbeing of the women involved.

"They're the ones who are impacted severely at the moment," he said, adding that the Swans did not want to interfere with the police investigation by reaching out to the women directly.

While the five suspended players will not be allowed to play for the rest of the year, Pavlich said "they will be allowed back at the football club" this season.

"We're not abandoning our players," he said.

"We are supporting our players through this really challenging time for them."

Pridham pointed out the sanctions should not tarnish the entire team's reputation.

"There are many players this doesn't apply to, and I believe our male team has, by and large, displayed complete respect for women, so I don't think that's something of concern," he said.

"However, clearly when situations such as this emerge, and clearly there has been a breakdown in standards, we will, in time, as a board and as an executive team, review how we deal with these things going forward and we'll look to see if changes need to be made.

"We're very, very proud of our culture. We don't get everything perfectly right over time, and things happen from time to time, and it's how we fix it going forward."

"I'd just highlight that this breach of our standards relates to five players. So, there are many players who this doesn't apply to," he said. "However, clearly, when situations such as this emerge – and clearly, there has been a breakdown in standards – we will, in time – as a board, and as an executive team – we will review how we deal with these things going forward." Club to be in a 'better position going forward', Pridham says Pridham has taken a question about whether he believes the Swans' season is now "torpedoed". "I think you've always got to enter the field of play with the expectation of performing well," he said. He says the fact that the club is willing to ban "five of our absolute best players" from the rest of the season shows it's "not trying to brush anything under the carpet". World.title: FIFA accused of 'management by fear' after key executive's sudden exit
World.content:
The head of Norwegian football has accused FIFA of fear tactics for the removal of a senior official who publicly opposed FIFA president Gianni Infantino's now-withdrawn World Cup sell-off plan.

Lise Klaveness, the head of the Norwegian Football Federation since 2022, told the Associated Press that the firing of FIFA's chief operating officer Kevin Lamour was "unacceptable" and urged other senior leaders to resist potentially damaging orders.

Mr Lamour's exit on Tuesday (AEST) came 17 days after his statement to AP criticising Mr Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.1 billion) private equity project, which was withdrawn hours later.

FIFA executive who criticised Infantino's World Cup sale plan departs FIFA's chief operating officer, Kevin Lamour, leaves soccer's governing body, weeks after publicly criticising president Gianni Infantino.

"Now he is thrown out and we are supposed to move on. It's unacceptable, it's management by fear," Ms Klaveness told the AP in a telephone interview, describing Mr Lamour as "the best football administrator I have ever met".

"Now we also have to call upon FIFA leadership and the administration to not submit to orders you know are not in the interests of football," Ms Klaveness added, especially targeting FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström.

Ms Klaveness represented Norway 73 times as a player, is a judge in Oslo and an elected executive committee member at European football body UEFA.

She has built on her country's long-held reputation as a champion of good governance in soccer.

Last week the Norwegian federation's board called on Mr Infantino to resign and has backed a London-based NGO's formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators about his political ties to US President Donald Trump.

Mr Lamour was a long-time colleague of Mr Infantino, first when they were senior officials at UEFA from 2007-15. He was involved in Mr Infantino's campaign to be elected FIFA president in 2016 and moved two years ago from UEFA to oversee much of FIFA's operations in Zurich.

Infantino in crisis

Kevin Lamour (centre) said FIFA staff were "deceived" by the World Cup sell-off plan. (Getty Images: Richard Sellers)

With a reputation among the most trusted executives in the often murky world of global football politics, Mr Lamour's pointed criticisms of Mr Infantino's leadership intensified a crisis for the FIFA president.

A backlash from UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation and north American soccer body CONCACAF was provoked by a secretive plan to sell future World Cup profits to investors led by Joshua Kushner.

A $4.2 billion investment to take a 20 per cent stake in a FIFA commercial spin-off was to fund offers of $20 million to each of its 211 national member federations.

They already effectively own the non-profit soccer body, which has multi-billion dollar reserves, and would have had a mid-September deadline to accept.

Mr Lamour's statement on July 31 spoke of FIFA staff being "deceived" by Mr Infantino's lack of openness over the now-failed sale and how they "deserve better than contempt and intimidation".

The French executive called on soccer leaders worldwide "to make the right decisions".

"If that means I lose my job, then so be it," he said at the conclusion of the statement.

"I will understand and respect that decision. At least I'll sleep well tonight."

'A firing situation'

Lise Klaveness with Gianni Infantino at last month's FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Eva Marie Uzcategui)

Ms Klaveness said Mr Lamour's exit was "a firing situation, it's not a resignation", and suggested it was done as a result of Mr Grafström "obviously being pressured by the president".

FIFA didn't respond to a request for comment on Ms Klaveness's remarks.

In a statement, FIFA said it "thanks Kevin for his two years of service and wishes him the best of luck for the future. No further comment will be made on the matter".

Mr Lamour did not immediately reply to an email seeking comment on Wednesday (AEST).

"His statement was necessary to kill the project," Ms Klaveness said of Mr Lamour's intervention.

" He said something that was obvious, that was very important that someone within the staff told us the story so that we knew it was not FIFA, as such, but one person. "

Mr Infantino held a meeting with senior management — minus Mr Lamour — in Rabat, Morocco on August 5.

Following that, FIFA issued a statement apologising for errors and said those managers who attended "reaffirmed their full support" for Mr Infantino's presidency.

"We all got reports in Morocco, we know it's a management of fear," Ms Klaveness said.

"It's not in football's best interests."

Until the uproar over Mr Infantino's "FIFA Forward Enterprise" proposal, he seemed sure to be re-elected unopposed next year in Morocco for a fourth and final term in office through 2031.

Challengers have until November 18 to enter the contest.

Norway not discussing other candidates

Though UEFA and other critics of Mr Infantino want him ousted from the $6 million-per-year FIFA job, Ms Klaveness said any search for an opponent was not a talking point in Norway.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We are not there at all and that is 100 per cent the truth," she said, adding that any candidate would have to be "very accountable to a governance structure that will not in four or five years just deteriorate".

Mr Infantino was appointed by UEFA in 2015 to a panel advising FIFA on reforms, in fallout from corruption scandals provoked by US federal investigations.

That group's recommendations limiting FIFA presidents to 12 years in office, plus limiting their executive powers and patronage all have retreated under Mr Infantino.

Ms Klaveness acknowledged FIFA members had been less "passionate about the details of governance" than Norway.

Mr Lamour also won praise and support from UEFA vice-president Laura McAllister, also a former player and now a university professor of governance in Wales, who lamented the "shabby events of the past weeks".

"Kevin's sacking seriously weakens FIFA's administration whilst undermining this unique opportunity to shift the culture at FIFA and to reset the organisation on sporting values, not simply commercial and financial ones," Ms McAllister said.

World.title: Dees star's ban upheld as AFL tribunal rejects biomechanist evidence bid
World.content:
Melbourne has suffered a major pre-finals blow, potentially losing key forward Jacob van Rooyen for the rest of the AFL season through suspension.

The Demons failed in their bid to have van Rooyen's three-game ban for striking overturned or reduced.

It means he will miss the fifth-placed Demons' final home-and-away game on Saturday against the Western Bulldogs, and that Melbourne will need to win two finals for him to play again this season.

Van Rooyen is having a career-best season, kicking 42 goals in 22 games.

The Demons forward was charged with striking after he concussed Port Adelaide defender Aliir Aliir in a marking contest on Saturday night at the Adelaide Oval. It was graded as severe impact, careless conduct and high impact.

After the 90-minute hearing, where van Rooyen testified that he was trying to mark the ball when he collected Aliir, the tribunal jury deliberated for nearly an hour before upholding the charge.

Melbourne had argued van Rooyen's attempt to mark the ball was not careless, but the tribunal rejected their case.

Tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC also turned down a bid from the Demons to have a biomechanist give evidence for van Rooyen.

Aliir Aliir was left concussed after being struck in the head by van Rooyen's swinging arm. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

"The swing of van Rooyen's left arm constituted the act of a strike. It was a forceful blow. It was not simply a trailing or leading arm that Aliir collided with," Gleeson said in the verdict, adding the panel found it was careless.

"Van Rooyen was initially intending to mark the ball, but we find that shortly before impact, he ceased to intend to mark the ball. We say this despite van Rooyen's evidence to the contrary.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"Even if it was van Rooyen's sole objective at all times to contest the mark, we find that he did so in a way that failed to take reasonable care to avoid acts which could be reasonably foreseen to result in a reportable offence.

"Van Rooyen had time to move his right arm in response to seeing Aliir and he could have done so to some extent or sufficient extent with his left arm."

The tribunal also found the impact was severe and said there was potential for further injury, such as a facial fracture.

Also on Tuesday night, Brisbane AFLW key forward Dakota Davidson failed to have her one-game striking ban downgraded.

The Lions pleaded guilty and tried to argue the clash with Essendon's Maddi Gay was low rather than medium impact, but the AFLW tribunal upheld the grading.

It means one of the league's top forwards will miss the grand final rematch against two-time defending premiers North Melbourne.

World.title: Venus Williams receives US Open wildcard at 46, Serena may follow
World.content:
Venus Williams has received a US Open singles wild card and the tournament is keeping one on hold, perhaps in case her sister Serena wants to join her.

Sloane Stephens, the 2017 US Open champion, was one of six other women to receive a wild card, and the US Tennis Association said the final one was still to be announced.

That will almost certainly go to Serena Williams if she decides she wants to return to the tournament at 44.

Venus Williams received a wild card last year, returning to the grand slam event she won twice for the first time since 2023. The 46-year-old has become the oldest entrant in singles at the tournament since Renee Richards played at 47 in 1981, according to the International Tennis Federation.

Serena Williams could make her return to Flushing Meadows via the final wildcard spot. (Getty Images: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport)

She has continued to play some singles matches, and this week joined Serena for their first doubles tournament together since the 2022 US Open. They lost at the Cincinnati Open in a match tiebreaker against Marta Kostyuk and Peyton Stearns.

The sisters planned to play at Wimbledon but had to withdraw after Serena injured her knee in her singles match. That marked her first time playing singles since the 2022 US Open, and she indicated afterwards that she hoped to keep competing if she was healthy.

Headlining the wild-card recipients on the men's side are 39-year-old Gael Monfils, a past US Open semifinalist who is set to play his final grand slam tournament before retiring, and Australian Alexei Popyrin, who upset Novak Djokovic in 2024 on the way to the fourth round.

One spot is also being held among the eight men's wild cards. Stan Wawrinka, the 2016 champion at Flushing Meadows, who at 41 is playing his final season, could be a candidate for that.

Australia's Alexei Popyrin has received one of the wildcards in the men's draw. (Getty Images: Icon Sportswire/David Kirouac)

Also receiving women's wild cards were Carol Young Suh Lee, Reese Brantmeier, Thea Frodin, Leolia Jeanjean and Taylah Preston.

The other men receiving wild cards were two-time reigning NCAA singles champion Michael Zheng, Martin Damm, JJ Wolf, Sebastian Gorzny and Jack Kennedy.

Kei Nishikori, the 2014 US Open runner-up who also is retiring, was given a wild card into the men's qualifying tournament, along with Jordan Lee, Trevor Svajda, Andre Ilagan, Spencer Johnson, Michael Antonius, Andrew Johnson and Daniel Milavsky.

Women given spots in the qualifying tournament were Caroline Dolehide, Janae Preston, Katrina Scott, Ayana Akli, Annika Penickova, Julieta Pareja, Kristina Penickova and Savannah Broadus.

The main draw begins on August 30, with the qualifying tournaments being played earlier that week.
